name: Particle diagram of an element, a compound or a mixture
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A rectangle (the container) holding 12 to 30 circles that never overlap. Element: all circles the same size and fill (single atoms), or joined pairs for a diatomic element such as H2 or O2. Compound: touching groups of two or three different circles in a fixed pattern (for example one large and two small for H2O). Mixture: two kinds of free particle, or a particle of an element and a particle of a compound, not bonded to each other. Kinds differ by size and by fill (white, hatched, grey) so that the picture survives photocopying (S12).
params: substance (element of atoms | element of molecules | compound | mixture of elements | mixture of compounds | mixture of element and compound), state (gas | liquid | solid), particle count (8 to 40), compound formula (AB | AB2 | A2B | ...)
scienceChecks: All particles of an element are one kind. Each compound particle holds at least two kinds of atom in the ratio of its formula (2 to 1 for H2O). A mixture has at least two kinds of particle and no bond between them. Circles never overlap.
notes: The same particle box serves the states-of-matter row (particleStates): one symbol with two uses.

name: Models of the atom: plum pudding, nuclear and shell
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: Plum pudding: a large circle with a pale fill, small electrons (marked with a minus sign) scattered inside it, and a label saying that the positive charge is spread through the ball. Nuclear model: a very small central dot or circle for the nucleus (marked with a plus sign) and a few electrons on a wide ring or on separate rings far out. Shell model: the nucleus with the concentric shells of bohrAtom. Labels: nucleus, electron, shell. A line says 'not to scale' on the nuclear and shell pictures.
params: model (plum pudding | nuclear | shell), number of electrons (1 to 10), show labels (boolean), electron mark (dot | cross | minus sign)
scienceChecks: The plum pudding picture has no separate nucleus. In the nuclear and shell pictures the nucleus is much smaller than the atom, and every electron is outside it. The electron count in the picture equals the count the parameter asks for.
notes: Read in the AQA summary of 4.1.1.3 and in an AQA paper that asks which diagram shows the plum pudding model. The AQA pages were read through the search tool, not as the PDF.

name: Alpha-particle scattering experiment
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: On the left a source of alpha particles in a lead block with a narrow slit. A straight beam to a thin gold foil drawn as a vertical strip of small circles (the atoms) with a tiny nucleus dot in each. A curved detector screen round the foil. About eight alpha paths drawn as arrows: most go straight through, two or three bend a little, one bounces back. Each path that bends is bent away from the nucleus it passes (like charges repel).
params: number of paths (5 to 12), show nuclei (boolean), show labels (boolean), show the plum pudding prediction in a second panel (boolean)
scienceChecks: A path that passes closer to a nucleus is bent more. Every bent path bends away from the nucleus. No path enters a nucleus. Most paths are straight. At most one path reverses.
notes: A drawn conclusion box ('most of the atom is empty space; the nucleus is small, dense and positive') is plain text.

name: Bohr model of an atom (electronic structure diagram)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: Concentric circles for the shells (radii about 28, 48, 68 and 88 u), the nucleus at the centre labelled with the symbol or with the numbers of protons and neutrons, and electrons as small dots or crosses spaced evenly round each ring. The shells fill 2, 8, 8, then the fourth shell (potassium and calcium). The structure can also be written as numbers (2,8,1) in a label.
params: element (Z 1 to 20), show nucleus contents (boolean: symbol only | protons and neutrons), electron mark (dot | cross), outer shell only (boolean), number string label (boolean)
scienceChecks: The electrons on the shells sum to Z. The shells fill 2, 8, 8, 2 in order, and an outer shell has electrons only if the shell inside it is full. The shell count equals the period number. The outer-shell count equals the group number (groups 1 to 7); helium has 2.
notes: 4.1.1.7 asks for the first twenty elements as numbers and as a diagram. The AQA wording was read through the search tool.

name: Electron arrangement of an ion (shell diagram in brackets)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: The shell diagram of bohrAtom for the ion: a metal ion has lost its outer shell, a non-metal ion has the electrons it gained added to its outer shell. The whole picture sits inside large square brackets with the charge written top right outside them (Na+, Mg2+, Cl-, O2-). Optional before-and-after pair joined by an arrow, the atom on the left and the ion on the right. The electrons that moved are drawn with a different mark (crosses for the gained ones).
params: element (Z 3 to 20), ion charge (automatic from the group, or set), show nucleus contents (boolean), show the atom before the ion (boolean), electron mark (dot | cross)
scienceChecks: Electrons = Z minus the charge for a positive ion, Z plus the size of the charge for a negative ion. The ion's shells match the nearest noble gas (2 | 2,8 | 2,8,8). The sign of the charge matches the element: metals positive, non-metals negative. Charge = protons minus electrons.
notes: Same engine as bohrAtom. The brackets and charge are the marks examiners look for.

name: Nuclear (isotope) notation with mass number and atomic number
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: The element symbol in 18 u text with two small stacked numbers at its left: the mass number above, the atomic number below, right-aligned with each other. An optional charge as a superscript at the right. An optional line under it, 'protons 11, neutrons 12, electrons 11'. The label markup has no stacked left-hand index, so this is a small text symbol.
params: element (Z 1 to 36), mass number (A), charge (optional, -3 to +3), show the particle counts (boolean)
scienceChecks: Mass number >= atomic number. Neutrons = A - Z and is not negative. The atomic number matches the element symbol from a table of the first 36 elements. Electrons = Z minus the charge.
notes: AQA 4.1.1.5 asks students to work out the particle numbers from the two numbers; the exact AQA figure was not visible in the text I read.

name: Isotopes drawn as nuclei (protons and neutrons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A tight cluster of circles for the nucleus: protons marked with a plus sign, neutrons plain. Two or three isotopes of one element side by side (for example hydrogen-1, -2 and -3, or chlorine-35 and -37), each under its nuclear notation. Clusters are packed hexagonally so that the number of circles is easy to count.
params: element (Z 1 to 18), mass numbers (one to three values), show notation (boolean), show counts (boolean)
scienceChecks: The proton count equals Z in every cluster and the neutron count equals A - Z. Isotopes of one element have the same Z and different A. Circles do not overlap. The total circles equal A.

name: Periodic table (outline with groups, periods and metal divider)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A grid of 18 columns and 7 rows of square cells (the f-block as two separate rows below). Each cell can show the symbol, the atomic number, the name or the relative atomic mass. Group numbers above (1 to 7 and 0, or 1 to 18), period numbers at the left. A stepped line separates metals from non-metals. Highlights: one group, one period, one element (a ring), the transition metals, or a block. Regions use a pattern as well as a fill so that they survive photocopying.
params: cell content (symbol | number | name | blank), range (first 20 | first 36 | all 118), highlight group, highlight period, highlight element, divider line (boolean), region shading (none | metal and non-metal | blocks), group numbering (0 to 7 | 1 to 18)
scienceChecks: The elements run in order of atomic number with the correct group and period. Helium is in group 0. The divider runs between the correct pairs of cells. Transition metals sit in groups 3 to 12 of periods 4 to 7. At most one highlight style is on a cell.
notes: It is a table, but a fixed 118-cell layout with highlight parameters, so it is classed as a symbol, not a chart. James to confirm.

name: Mendeleev's early periodic table with gaps
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A table of rows and columns of element symbols in order of atomic weight with a few question marks where elements were then unknown (the gaps that predicted gallium and germanium). Used as a source in a question, seldom drawn by a student.
params: show the gaps (boolean), highlight swapped pairs such as tellurium and iodine (boolean)
scienceChecks: none
notes: Table: outside PracDraw unless James brings tables into scope. Content is from memory.

name: Table of relative charge and mass of the subatomic particles
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A three-row table: proton (relative charge +1, relative mass 1), neutron (0, 1), electron (-1, very small, about 1/1835). Usually a 'complete the table' question.
params: show answers (boolean), which cells are blank
scienceChecks: Charges sum to zero for a neutral atom with equal protons and electrons. The mass of the electron is shown as very small, never as 1.
notes: Table: outside PracDraw unless James brings tables into scope. From memory; a text box with a ruled grid in the editor does the job today.

name: A Group 1 metal reacting with water
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A trough or a large beaker of water (Water preset, 60 %). A small piece of metal (the irregularSolid symbol made small and pale grey) on the surface, a few bubbles under it, and an optional lit splint above the bubbles. With universal indicator the liquid is the Purple preset to show an alkali. A label gives the metal and the gas (hydrogen).
params: container (trough | beaker), metal (lithium | sodium | potassium), indicator colour (boolean), splint (boolean)
scienceChecks: The metal sits on the liquid surface, not in it. Bubbles are under or beside the piece. If the indicator is on, the liquid is purple or blue, never red or green.
notes: A new template from existing symbols (trough, beaker, irregularSolid, splint). Schools often show a video, so the picture is for a worksheet.

name: Halogen displacement reactions in test tubes
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: Use the testTubeReactions template with three or four tubes in a rack. Tubes hold potassium chloride, bromide or iodide solution (Colourless solution preset) and, after adding a halogen water, the Orange preset (bromine) or the Brown preset (iodine). Label each tube with the pair of chemicals. A tube where nothing happens keeps its first colour.
params: pairs of halogen and halide (Cl2 or Br2 or I2 with Cl- or Br- or I-), result colours
scienceChecks: A displacement happens only when the added halogen is higher in the group than the halide ion (Cl2 with Br- or I-; Br2 with I-). A non-reaction tube keeps its first colour. Bromine water is orange and iodine solution is brown.
notes: No new code. The colour presets already exist.

name: Graph of a property down a group (melting or boiling point)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A line graph or bar chart of melting point or boiling point against the elements of Group 1 or Group 7, used to predict a missing value. Axes, scale and plotted points.
params: group (1 | 7), property, which value is missing
scienceChecks: The trend is monotonic: melting and boiling points fall down Group 1 and rise down Group 7.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. From memory.

name: Particle diagrams of a solid, a liquid and a gas
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three boxes side by side. Solid: touching circles in a regular lattice, with small vibration marks. Liquid: touching circles in an irregular arrangement filling the lower part of the box, with a few short motion arrows. Gas: widely spaced circles all through the box, with longer arrows in random directions. Each box has a one-line label (arrangement, movement) when asked. Circles do not overlap.
params: state (solid | liquid | gas), particle count (10 to 40), particle kind (atom | pair | triple), show motion arrows (boolean), show labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: A solid is a regular lattice in contact. A liquid has contact without regular rows. A gas has gaps larger than a particle diameter. The three boxes show the same number of particles. Circles never overlap.
notes: The same symbol as particleElementCompoundMixture. Exam questions ask students to state limitations of this model (spacing and size not to scale, no forces shown), which is text.

name: Changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, sublimation)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three particle boxes (solid, liquid, gas) in a row with a pair of labelled arrows between solid and liquid (melting above, freezing below) and between liquid and gas (boiling or evaporating above, condensing below). An optional long curved arrow from solid to gas for sublimation. Arrows are labelled with the change of state and, optionally, 'energy in' on the upward arrows and 'energy out' on the downward ones.
params: show sublimation (boolean), show energy labels (boolean), label mode (names | blank for a worksheet)
scienceChecks: Melting, boiling and sublimation arrows carry 'energy in'; freezing and condensing carry 'energy out'. The boxes use the particleStates arrangements. The arrows join the correct pairs of boxes.

name: Heating and cooling curve of a pure substance
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Axes: temperature (vertical) against time (horizontal). A line that rises, flattens at the melting point, rises again, flattens at the boiling point, rises again; regions labelled solid, solid and liquid, liquid, liquid and gas, gas. The cooling curve is the reverse.
params: direction (heating | cooling), substance (generic | water), show state labels (boolean), show particle boxes under each region (boolean)
scienceChecks: The flat sections lie at the melting point and the boiling point. The temperature never falls during heating. The boiling-point plateau is higher than the melting-point plateau.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. The priority is how often it is drawn, not a build order. A particle box under each region would use particleStates.

name: Dot-and-cross diagram of an ionic compound
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Two forms. Transfer: the metal atom and the non-metal atom as circles for their outer shells, the metal's electrons as dots and the non-metal's as crosses, with curved arrows showing the electrons moving across. Ions: each ion inside large square brackets with its charge top right outside them; the metal ion shows its full inner shell only (or no outer electrons), the non-metal ion a full outer shell of dots and crosses. For MgCl2 or Na2O the second ion is drawn beside the first with the ratio visible. Inner shells are optional and, when drawn, appear as plain circles.
params: metal (Li | Na | K | Mg | Ca), non-metal (O | S | F | Cl | Br), stage (transfer | ions), show inner shells (boolean), mark style (dot and cross | all dots)
scienceChecks: Electrons lost by the metal atoms equal electrons gained by the non-metal atoms. Each ion has the electron structure of a noble gas. The charge follows the group number (group 1 +1, group 2 +2, group 6 -2, group 7 -1). The numbers of ions give a neutral compound.
notes: AQA 4.2.1.2 limits the examples to Group 1 and 2 metals with Group 6 and 7 non-metals. Brackets and charges are what a mark scheme rewards. Decision for James: whether every picture uses dots for one atom and crosses for the other, and whether another pair of marks is allowed for photocopy-safe prints.

name: Dot-and-cross diagram of a simple covalent molecule
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: One circle for the outer shell of each atom, overlapping where atoms are bonded. Each shared pair sits in the overlap as one dot and one cross. The other outer electrons of each atom stay on its own circle as dots or crosses, with lone pairs drawn as pairs. The central atom is in the middle for H2O, NH3, CH4 and CO2. Double and triple bonds have two and three pairs in the overlap. Inner shells are never drawn. A second layout puts the atoms apart with the shared pairs between them.
params: molecule (H2 | Cl2 | O2 | N2 | HCl | H2O | NH3 | CH4 are the eight in the specification; CO2 | HF | F2 | C2H4 | C2H6 as extras), layout (overlapping circles | circles apart), mark style (dot and cross | all dots)
scienceChecks: Every atom ends with a full outer shell (2 for hydrogen, 8 for the others). The shared pairs equal the usual valency (H 1, Cl 1, O 2, N 3, C 4). The total outer electrons equal the sum over the atoms (8 for H2O, 8 for NH3, 8 for CH4). Lone pairs are shown. Each shared pair has one dot and one cross.
notes: AQA names eight molecules. Examiners expect lone pairs to be shown. A dot-and-cross shows no shape; that limitation is part of the specification.

name: Displayed formula of a small molecule (lines for bonds)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Atom symbols in 15 u text joined by single lines, double lines or triple lines, laid out flat with the bonds at right angles or at 120 degrees (the 2D convention, not the real shape). Hydrogen atoms are shown. Used for H2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4, CO2, N2, O2 and the first alkanes.
params: molecule (from a list of 12 small molecules), show lone pairs (boolean), show the molecular formula under it (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each atom has the number of bonds of its valency (H 1, O 2, N 3, C 4, Cl 1). The count of each element equals the molecular formula. Double and triple bonds drawn as two and three parallel lines.
notes: The same bond graph also feeds the ball-and-stick and the organic displayed-formula rows. One molecule engine, several drawings.

name: Ball-and-stick model of a small molecule
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Spheres joined by sticks, drawn as circles with a small highlight line (no shading, no gradient, S7) and sticks as two parallel lines in an oblique view. Methane tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal, water bent, carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride linear. Atoms are told apart by size and by a hatch or grey fill, with a key (symbol and fill) beside the model.
params: molecule (from the list of 12 small molecules), view (front | oblique), show key (boolean), show element labels on the balls (boolean)
scienceChecks: The number of balls of each element equals the formula. Each ball has its valency of sticks. Bond angles in the model: 109.5 for CH4, about 107 for NH3, about 104.5 for H2O, 180 for CO2 and HCl. Key matches the fills used.
notes: AQA asks students to name limitations of ball-and-stick models (the sticks suggest physical links, sizes are not to scale). Decision for James: how a 3D model is drawn in a 2D line style (oblique projection).

name: Space-filling model of a small molecule
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Overlapping circles at the atom positions with the nearer atoms drawn in front, and a key for the atoms. No sticks. Mentioned beside dot-and-cross and ball-and-stick when students compare models.
params: molecule (from the list of 12 small molecules), show key (boolean)
scienceChecks: The number of circles of each element equals the formula. Circle sizes follow the relative sizes of the atoms (H smaller than O smaller than Cl).

name: Giant ionic lattice in two dimensions
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A square grid of touching circles in alternating kinds: the positive ions small and marked +, the negative ions larger and marked -. Usually 4 by 4 to 6 by 6, with a wavy edge or open ends to show that it goes on. A ball-and-stick variant joins neighbours with short lines. Optional ion labels (Na+ and Cl-). For a 1 to 2 compound the layout is staggered, so that a student can count the ratio and give the empirical formula.
params: compound ratio (1 to 1 | 1 to 2 | 2 to 1), ion labels (Na+ and Cl- | Mg2+ and O2- | custom), grid size (3 to 8), style (balls | ball-and-stick | open ends), show charges (boolean)
scienceChecks: No two like ions touch in a 1 to 1 grid. Counting the ions of each kind in the complete repeating unit gives the ratio of the formula. The total charge of the repeating unit is zero. Ion sizes: negative ions drawn larger for the common cases.
notes: AQA names only sodium chloride, but asks students to deduce the formula from a diagram.

name: Sodium chloride lattice in three dimensions (ball and stick)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A 3 by 3 by 3 cube of alternating small (Na+) and large (Cl-) circles in an oblique projection: the front face drawn square and the back face shifted up and right at half size, joined by lines. Hidden back bonds are thinner or dashed. A variant highlights one central ion and its six neighbours of the opposite kind. The ions are marked + and - and labelled.
params: size (2 by 2 by 2 | 3 by 3 by 3), highlight one ion and its neighbours (boolean), show labels (boolean), hidden lines (dashed | none)
scienceChecks: No two like ions are nearest neighbours along an edge. The highlighted ion has six nearest neighbours of the opposite kind. In a 3 by 3 by 3 block there are 14 ions of one kind and 13 of the other.
notes: Decision for James: the style of 3D structures in a 2D line drawing. Oblique projection with dashed hidden lines is proposed; the same projection serves diamond, ice and iodine.

name: Metallic bonding (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Rows of equal circles marked + (the metal ions) in a regular lattice, with small dots or minus signs scattered in the gaps between them (the delocalised electrons, drawn irregularly, not in rows). Optional arrows on the electrons for conduction, and optional displaced rows with a slip arrow to show why metals bend.
params: metal (generic | sodium | magnesium | aluminium), rows (3 to 6), columns (4 to 8), show conduction arrows (boolean), show a slip arrow (boolean)
scienceChecks: The delocalised electrons per ion equal the group number (1, 2 or 3), counted over the drawn region. The ion charge equals that number. The ions are one size, regularly spaced. Nothing joins the ions with lines.
notes: Wording of the specification: students recognise metallic structures from diagrams of their bonding.

name: Alloy and pure metal layers (why alloys are harder)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Rows of equal circles for the pure metal, with a heavy arrow showing one layer sliding over the next. The alloy picture is the same lattice with some circles replaced by a larger (or smaller) kind, so the rows are pushed out of line, and the sliding arrow is crossed out. Foreign atoms differ by size and by fill.
params: mode (pure metal | alloy), foreign atom size (larger | smaller), foreign fraction (5 to 30 percent), layers (4 to 7), show slip arrows (boolean)
scienceChecks: The pure picture has one size of circle in straight rows. The alloy picture has at least two sizes and no overlapping circles. The foreign fraction is within the set value.

name: Diamond (giant covalent, tetrahedral)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Carbon atoms (small circles) joined by single lines, each atom bonded to four neighbours in a tetrahedral pattern, in an oblique projection with the rear bonds lighter or dashed. Three sizes: one atom with its four bonds; a cluster of about 14 atoms; a 2D flat network version. Edge atoms end in short stubs, not open bonds. A label gives 'each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds'.
params: extent (one atom | cluster of 14 | cell of 18), view (oblique | flat network), show bond angle (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every interior carbon has four bonds. Bond lengths are equal in the model. The angle between bonds from one atom is 109.5 degrees in the 3D model before projection. No ring has other than six atoms in the cluster.
notes: The specification asks students to explain the properties of diamond, not to draw it; exam figures still show it for recognition.

name: Graphite (layers of hexagons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three stacked layers drawn as flat parallelograms in oblique view, each a network of carbon hexagons with atoms at the corners. The top layer is fully drawn, the lower ones are simpler. The gap between layers has dotted lines for the weak forces. Optional dots above one layer for the delocalised electrons. Labels: layer, weak forces, delocalised electron.
params: layers (2 to 4), hexagons per layer shown (4 to 7), show weak forces (boolean), show delocalised electrons (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every atom in a layer has three bonds at 120 degrees and every ring has six atoms. The spacing between layers is clearly larger than a bond. The weak forces are dotted or dashed, never drawn as bonds.

name: Graphene (one layer of hexagons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A flat honeycomb of carbon hexagons, about 4 rows by 5 columns, atoms at the vertices and bonds as lines, with short stubs or a wavy cut line at the edge. A label gives 'one atom thick'. An optional side-view inset is a single row of circles.
params: rows (3 to 6), columns (3 to 7), show atoms as dots (boolean), side view inset (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every interior atom has three bonds at 120 degrees. Every ring has six atoms. No ring of another size appears.

name: Buckminsterfullerene C60
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A ball of 60 carbon atoms joined by lines: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, each pentagon surrounded by hexagons. Two views: the visible hemisphere with the rear half in a lighter line, or a flat Schlegel-style network with the outer face as the big outline. Label 'C60'. Hollow.
params: view (ball | flat network), show atoms (boolean), shade the pentagons (boolean)
scienceChecks: 60 vertices, 90 edges, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons (the vertices minus the edges plus the faces equal 2). Every atom has three bonds. Each pentagon touches only hexagons.
notes: The hardest of the carbon pictures to draw by hand; it should be a generated symbol, not hand-edited.

name: Carbon nanotube
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A cylinder made by rolling the graphene honeycomb, in oblique view: an open or capped end ellipse, the hexagon network on the visible surface, atoms at the vertices. A label gives 'nanotube'. The length is several times the diameter.
params: length in rings (3 to 8), circumference in hexagons (6 to 10), capped ends (boolean), show atoms (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every atom has three bonds. The hexagon pattern wraps round the tube without a gap or an overlap. Length is at least three times the diameter.

name: Silicon dioxide (giant covalent)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: The diamond network with an oxygen atom drawn in the middle of every bond between two silicon atoms. Silicon atoms larger, oxygen smaller, different fills, with a key. Flat 2D network or a 3D cluster of about 5 silicon atoms. Edge atoms end in stubs.
params: view (flat network | oblique cluster), show key (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every silicon has four oxygen neighbours and every oxygen has two silicon neighbours. No Si-Si or O-O bond. The ratio of silicon to oxygen in a large interior region is 1 to 2.

name: Polymer chains (linear, branched and cross-linked)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Several long zig-zag chains of carbon atoms side by side, with hydrogen stubs. Linear chains (HDPE) lie close and parallel. Branched chains (LDPE) have short side chains that keep neighbours apart. Cross-linked chains (thermosetting) have short bridges between chains. Dotted lines between chains show the weak forces. Optional repeating unit in square brackets.
params: type (linear | branched | cross-linked), chains (3 to 6), branch frequency, show weak forces (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every carbon in a chain has two chain bonds and two other bonds. Branches are attached to chain carbons only. Cross-links join two different chains. Linear chains lie closer together than branched ones.
notes: A past AQA paper, reported through the search tool, shows part of the structures of HDPE and LDPE and asks why HDPE is denser. I could not tell which paper, so the row is secondary.

name: Why ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three particle boxes of + and - ions: solid (ions fixed in a lattice), molten (ions close together but free), dissolved (ions spread apart in water, with water drawn as plain background). Under each, a small cell and bulb symbol that is off for the solid and lit for the other two, or a label 'ions cannot move' and 'ions free to move'.
params: show circuit symbol (boolean), show labels (boolean), compound label
scienceChecks: The solid box is a regular lattice; the other two are not. Positive and negative ions are present in the same numbers in every box (charge balance). The bulb is lit only when the ions are free.

name: Cubes for surface area to volume ratio (nanoparticles and rates)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Cubes of side 1, 2 and 3 units (or one cube cut into 8 smaller cubes) in an oblique view, with grid squares on the visible faces, the side length on an edge, and a line of text under each giving the surface area, the volume and the ratio. The same cubes show why a powder reacts faster than a lump.
params: side lengths (1 to 4 values), cut one cube into n by n by n cubes (boolean), show grid squares (boolean), show values (boolean)
scienceChecks: Surface area = 6 x side squared, volume = side cubed, and the printed ratio equals 6 over the side. Cutting a cube into n cubed smaller cubes keeps the volume and multiplies the surface area by n.
notes: 4.2.4 may be chemistry only (not in Trilogy). Course membership is from my memory of the chemistry-only labels and should be checked. The same drawing serves the surface-area factor in rates.

name: Size scale: atoms, nanoparticles and cells on a powers-of-ten line
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A horizontal line marked in powers of ten from 0.1 nm to 1 mm with labelled objects: atom, small molecule, nanoparticle range (1 to 100 nm), virus, bacterium, cell, hair width. A scale diagram with no data.
params: range of the scale, which objects are shown or blanked
scienceChecks: Each object sits at its size on the log line. Nanoparticles span 1 to 100 nm. Each tick is ten times the last.
notes: A scale line, not a graph of data; classed chart because it is a labelled axis. Course membership and sizes are from memory.

name: Mass change in an open and a closed flask on a balance
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the massLoss template: a conical flask on the balance with marble chips, acid and bubbles, a cotton wool plug in the neck, and the balance reading as text. Draw it twice side by side for 'before' and 'after' with readings such as 150.00 g and 149.20 g. For a closed system swap the cotton wool plug for a bung and give both pictures the same reading.
params: open or closed (cotton wool plug or bung), reading before and after (text), reaction mixture contents
scienceChecks: With a gas product and an open flask the second reading is lower than the first. A closed flask has equal readings. Both readings use the same unit and number of decimal places.
notes: AQA 4.3 asks students to explain apparent mass changes in non-enclosed systems; the search summary of the AQA page does not say a diagram is required, but exam questions and every textbook use this picture.

name: Heating magnesium in a crucible with a lid (mass gain)
subject: chemistry
draw: A crucible with a lid on a pipeclay triangle on a tripod, a Bunsen burner with a blue flame under it on a heatproof mat, a coil of magnesium ribbon inside the crucible, and a label 'lift the lid briefly to let air in'. Optional pair of balance readings before and after (the oxide is heavier).
params: lid (on | slightly raised), flame (blue | off), show balance readings (boolean)
scienceChecks: The crucible stands on the triangle, not on the gauze. The flame is under the crucible. The ribbon is inside the crucible. The after reading is larger than the before reading because oxygen has joined the metal.
notes: A new template from existing symbols (crucible, pipeclayTriangle, tripod, bunsenBurner, heatproofMat, magnesiumRibbon). Tongs are in the Later list and are not needed.

name: A balanced equation drawn with particle models
subject: chemistry
draw: Each formula in the equation drawn as a small ball-and-stick model, the number of models equal to the coefficient, with plus signs and a reaction arrow between the groups. Atoms are told apart by size and fill with a key. Under each group the formula is written. For a worksheet some models can be blanked for the student to complete.
params: reaction (2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O | N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 | CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O | H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl | C + O2 -> CO2 | 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO), show formulae (boolean), blank models (0 to 3)
scienceChecks: For every element the number of drawn atoms on the left equals the number on the right. Each model matches its formula. The number of models equals the coefficient.
notes: Uses the ball-and-stick engine of the molecules pack.

name: Limiting reactant shown with particle models (before and after)
subject: chemistry
draw: A box before the reaction with, for example, 6 hydrogen molecules and 2 nitrogen molecules, an arrow, and a box after with the ammonia formed and the reactant left over. Models as in balancedEquationModels. Used for the Higher Tier idea of a limiting reactant.
params: reaction, number of molecules of each reactant (1 to 10), show the leftover (computed)
scienceChecks: Products formed = the smallest of (available divided by coefficient) times the product coefficient. Leftover counts are not negative. Atoms are conserved from the before box to the after box.
notes: Higher Tier idea; the picture is from memory of how teachers show it. The AQA search summary names limiting reactants but not a diagram.

name: Dilute and concentrated solutions as particle pictures
subject: chemistry
draw: Two or three boxes or beakers of equal volume, each showing the same number of water background and a different number of solute particles (circles). Labels: dilute, concentrated, and the amount of solute per dm3 under each. Water is the plain background and is not drawn as particles.
params: boxes (2 or 3), solute particles in each (2 to 40), concentration label (g per dm3 | mol per dm3), show labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: The boxes have equal volume. The ratio of the particle counts equals the ratio of the labelled concentrations. Particles do not overlap.
notes: Same picture serves the concentration factor in rates.

name: Reading a burette or measuring cylinder (enlarged scale)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the magnified scale: a section of a burette or measuring cylinder with divisions and the end values, a liquid with a meniscus, and the reading set with the Reading field. The student writes the reading to the nearest half division. Blank mode removes the answer.
params: top, bottom, divisions, unit, liquid level (reading)
scienceChecks: The reading is the bottom of the meniscus. On a burette the numbers increase downwards. The reading is a multiple of half a division.
notes: Reading scales is a skill in the titration practical.

name: Titration apparatus (burette, flask and white tile)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the titration template: a burette clamped upright with its tip inside the neck of a conical flask, the flask on a white tile with alkali and an indicator (Pink preset for phenolphthalein), labels for each part. Add the volumetricPipette and pipetteFiller beside it for the stage where the alkali is measured.
params: indicator (phenolphthalein | methyl orange), burette reading, flask contents colour, label mode
scienceChecks: The burette is upright, clamped, and its tip is above the liquid in the flask. A tile is under the flask. The indicator colour matches the stage of the titration: phenolphthalein pink in alkali, colourless at the end point; methyl orange yellow in alkali, orange or red at the end point.
notes: Required practical 2 of 8462 (chemistry only). AQA's own sheet uses methyl orange; the template shows phenolphthalein.

name: Table of titration results (rough, trials, mean titre)
subject: chemistry
draw: A ruled table with columns for rough, trial 1, trial 2 and trial 3, and rows for final burette reading, initial reading and titre (cm3), with a line for the mean of the concordant titres. Often partly filled for a student to complete.
params: number of trials, which cells are filled, units
scienceChecks: Titre = final minus initial reading. Concordant titres lie within 0.10 cm3. The mean uses concordant titres only.
notes: Table: outside PracDraw unless James brings tables into scope. From memory of the required practical.

name: Reactivity series (ordered list with carbon and hydrogen)
subject: chemistry
draw: A vertical list of metals from most to least reactive (potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, then carbon for reference, zinc, iron, hydrogen for reference, copper, silver, gold) with an arrow along the side labelled 'more reactive'. Optionally the method of extraction beside each part: electrolysis above carbon, reduction with carbon below it. Boxes can be blanked for an ordering task.
params: which metals are shown, show carbon and hydrogen (boolean), show extraction methods (boolean), blank positions
scienceChecks: The order is K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, (C), Zn, Fe, (H), Cu, Ag, Au. A metal above carbon is extracted by electrolysis; a metal below carbon can be reduced with carbon.
notes: A list, not a graph of data. Outside PracDraw unless James brings lists and tables into scope; the text tool does the job today. Priority A is how often it is used in lessons.

name: Metals in dilute acid in test tubes (rate of bubbling)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the testTubeReactions template with four tubes in a rack, each with a small piece of a different metal (the metal ribbon symbol, labelled) in Colourless solution. Bubbles: many in magnesium, fewer in zinc, few in iron, none in copper. Labels name the metals and the acid. Optional gas test above one tube.
params: metals shown, bubbles per tube (none | few | many)
scienceChecks: The amount of bubbling falls down the reactivity series. Copper has no bubbles. The gas given off is hydrogen.
notes: No new code.

name: Displacement of a metal from a salt solution
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the testTubeReactions template: tubes with a metal strip or an iron nail in copper sulfate solution (Blue preset) before and after, the blue fading and a brown deposit (a powder layer) on the metal; a tube with no change for a less reactive metal. Labels give the metals and the solution.
params: pairs of metal and salt solution, before or after, deposit on or off
scienceChecks: A displacement happens only if the added metal is more reactive than the metal in the salt. The blue colour fades only when copper ions are used up. The deposit is the less reactive metal.
notes: There is no copper-coloured powder preset; the nearest is the orange-brown precipitate. A preset would help.

name: Heating a metal oxide with carbon and testing the gas
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the thermalDecomposition template with a black mixture of copper oxide and carbon (Black powder preset) in the boiling tube, the delivery tube into limewater in a test tube, and the Bunsen under the powder. Optional labels: 'copper oxide and carbon', 'limewater turns cloudy'.
params: powder colour and label, limewater state (clear | cloudy)
scienceChecks: The tube is open at one point only (the delivery tube end in the limewater, S13). The delivery tube end dips below the limewater surface. The limewater turns cloudy because carbon dioxide forms.
notes: Reduction with carbon is named in 4.4.1.3; the apparatus is a classroom choice, not an AQA figure.

name: Blast furnace for the extraction of iron
subject: chemistry
draw: A tall furnace outline, wide in the middle and narrower at top and bottom. Inlets: iron ore, coke and limestone at the top, hot air blown in near the bottom. Outlets: waste gases at the top, molten slag (the lighter layer) and molten iron (the heavier layer) tapped at the bottom. Temperature rises downwards (arrows). Key reactions as labels: carbon burns to carbon dioxide; carbon dioxide and carbon give carbon monoxide; iron(III) oxide and carbon monoxide give iron and carbon dioxide; limestone breaks down and the calcium oxide forms slag with silica.
params: show equations (boolean), show temperatures (boolean), blank labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: Solids enter at the top and air at the bottom. Slag sits above the molten iron. The equation Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 is balanced. The equation CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 is balanced.
notes: The AQA text I read asks for reduction with carbon and does not name the furnace; the picture is a teaching and textbook diagram. Check whether James wants it.

name: Preparing a pure dry soluble salt (react, filter, evaporate)
subject: chemistry
draw: Three pictures in order, all existing templates. Step 1, heatingBeaker: warm dilute acid in a beaker on a gauze, with the insoluble oxide or carbonate added in excess and stirred (glass rod). Step 2, filtration: funnel and filter paper over a conical flask, the unreacted solid on the paper. Step 3, crystallisation (the evaporating basin on a beaker of water or on the gauze). Labels name each step.
params: salt (copper sulfate from copper oxide and sulfuric acid), step 1, 2 or 3
scienceChecks: The base is in excess (solid left in the beaker). The funnel stem is in the flask mouth. The solution is heated gently to concentrate, not to dryness.
notes: Required practical 1 of 8462 and 8 of Trilogy. Three existing templates in sequence; no new code.

name: pH scale with universal indicator colours
subject: chemistry
draw: A horizontal strip divided into 15 cells numbered 0 to 14, coloured red, orange, yellow, green (7) then blue and purple, with a bracket for acidic below 7, neutral at 7 and alkaline above 7. Optional examples at their positions (lemon juice, water, soap, bleach). Colours are test colours; every cell also carries its number so the picture survives photocopying.
params: orientation (horizontal | vertical), show numbers (boolean), show acid and alkali brackets (boolean), show example substances (boolean), blank labels
scienceChecks: pH values rise from 0 to 14 in order. The colour order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. Acidic is below 7, alkaline above 7, neutral at 7.
notes: Band edges differ between sources (strong acid pH 0 to 2 or 1 to 3), so the row keeps the bands as parameters.

name: Strong and weak acids as particle pictures
subject: chemistry
draw: Two boxes of the same size and the same number of acid particles. Strong acid: every molecule split into H+ and a negative ion (fully ionised). Weak acid: mostly whole molecules, with a few H+ and negative ions, and a reversible arrow between the formula forms. Water is the plain background.
params: acid (hydrochloric | ethanoic), particles (10 to 30), fraction ionised (strong 100 percent | weak 5 to 20 percent), show reversible arrow (boolean)
scienceChecks: A strong acid has no whole molecules left. A weak acid has more whole molecules than ions. The numbers of H+ and of negative ions are equal. Hydrogen atoms are conserved: whole molecules plus H+ ions equal the starting number of molecules.
notes: Higher Tier idea in 8462 (4.4.2.5). Strength is not the same as concentration.

name: Electrolysis cell with the movement of ions
subject: chemistry
draw: A cell holding the electrolyte (molten or a solution), two electrodes joined by wires to a power supply, the negative electrode (cathode) and positive electrode (anode) marked. Ions are labelled circles in the liquid with arrows: positive ions towards the cathode, negative ions towards the anode. The products are labelled at each electrode (a metal coating, or bubbles of a named gas). Optional half-equations for Higher Tier and electron arrows in the wires.
params: electrolyte (molten lead bromide | sodium chloride solution | copper sulfate solution | copper chloride solution | sodium sulfate solution), electrodes (inert | copper), show ions (boolean), show products (boolean), show half-equations (boolean), electron arrows (boolean)
scienceChecks: Positive ions move to the negative electrode and negative ions to the positive electrode. The products follow the rules: at the cathode a metal if it is less reactive than hydrogen, else hydrogen; at the anode a halogen if a halide is present, else oxygen. Half-equations balance in atoms and charge (Pb2+ + 2e- -> Pb; 2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-).
notes: AQA asks students to show ion movement and to write half-equations (Higher Tier). The product rules are in 4.4.3.4.

name: Apparatus for electrolysis of a molten compound
subject: chemistry
draw: A crucible (or a deep basin) of the molten compound on a pipeclay triangle on a tripod, a Bunsen burner under it on a heatproof mat. Two graphite electrodes held from above by clamps, dipping into the liquid without touching each other or the bottom, wires with crocodile clips to a power supply and a lamp or an ammeter. A label says that the work is done in a fume cupboard.
params: compound (lead bromide | zinc chloride), electrodes (graphite), show lamp (boolean)
scienceChecks: The electrodes dip into the liquid and do not touch each other. The flame is under the crucible. The circuit runs from the supply through both electrodes and back.
notes: AQA names lead bromide and suggests anhydrous zinc chloride as a safer choice. The apparatus is not in the required practical.

name: Electrolysis of a solution with gas collected in inverted tubes
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the electrolysis template: the cell with two electrodes, two upside-down test tubes over the electrodes, gas in both tubes with about twice the volume over the negative electrode for a sodium sulfate solution, wires to a power supply. Label the electrodes + and -, and the gases.
params: solution, gas volumes in the two tubes
scienceChecks: Hydrogen collects at the negative electrode and has twice the volume of the oxygen at the positive electrode for dilute sodium sulfate. The tube mouths are below the liquid surface.

name: Electrolysis of an aqueous solution with a Petri dish lid (required practical)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the electrolysisBeaker template: a beaker of solution with a lid on its rim, a carbon rod through each of two holes, a crocodile clip on the top of each rod, wires to a low-voltage supply. A strip of blue litmus paper held at the anode for chlorine. Labels: carbon electrodes, solution, supply.
params: solution (copper chloride | copper sulfate | sodium chloride | sodium sulfate), litmus paper (boolean)
scienceChecks: The electrodes dip into the solution and do not touch. The supply voltage label is low (4 V or less). Litmus is held in the gas, not in the liquid.
notes: Required practical 3 of 8462 and 9 of Trilogy.

name: Electrolysis cell for the extraction of aluminium
subject: chemistry
draw: A section of a rectangular steel tank lined with carbon along the bottom and sides (the negative electrode). A layer of molten aluminium at the bottom with a tap hole, above it the electrolyte (aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite). Two or three carbon blocks hang from the top (the positive electrodes) with bubbles of oxygen rising and a gas outlet. Wires to a power supply. Labels for each part.
params: show labels (boolean), show half-equations (boolean), blank labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: The anodes are the positive carbon blocks above and the cathode is the tank lining. Aluminium collects at the bottom (it is denser than the electrolyte). Oxygen forms at the anodes and burns the carbon away, so the anodes are replaced. Half-equations balance: Al3+ + 3e- -> Al; 2O2- -> O2 + 4e-; overall 2Al2O3 -> 4Al + 3O2.
notes: AQA asks why a mixture with cryolite is used and why the positive electrodes are replaced.

name: Electrolytic purification of copper
subject: chemistry
draw: A tank of copper sulfate solution with a thick block of impure copper as the positive electrode and a thin sheet of pure copper as the negative electrode, wires to a power supply. The anode is shown eaten away with a little sludge below it; the cathode is shown thicker with a coat of copper. Copper ions drawn as arrows from the anode to the cathode.
params: show ions (boolean), show half-equations (boolean), before or after
scienceChecks: The anode loses mass and the cathode gains the same mass of copper. The copper ion concentration stays constant. Half-equations: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e- at the anode; Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu at the cathode.
notes: Not named in the AQA text I read except as electrolysis with copper electrodes.

name: Reaction profile (energy level diagram): exothermic and endothermic
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes: 'Energy' up the side and 'Progress of reaction' along the bottom, with no numbers. A smooth curve from a flat reactants level up to a rounded peak and down to a flat products level. Exothermic: products below the reactants. Endothermic: products above. Each level is labelled (reactants, products, or their formulae). A double-headed arrow from the reactants level to the peak is the activation energy. A vertical arrow between the two levels is the overall energy change, pointing down for exothermic and up for endothermic. Option: a second, lower, dashed hump for the catalysed pathway.
params: type (exothermic | endothermic), catalyst (boolean), show activation energy arrow (boolean), show overall change arrow (boolean), level labels (words | formulae), blank labels for a worksheet (boolean)
scienceChecks: Exothermic: products below reactants. Endothermic: products above. The peak is above both levels. The activation energy arrow starts at the reactants level and ends at the peak. The overall change arrow runs from the reactants level to the products level. The catalysed peak is lower and the start and end levels are unchanged. The line is a smooth curve.
notes: AQA asks students to draw simple profiles with a curved line and to complete part-drawn ones with labels. The catalyst version is also asked in the rates section. The AQA pages were read through the search tool.

name: Bond breaking and bond making (bond energy calculation)
subject: chemistry
draw: The reaction as displayed formulae in a row (for example H-H plus Cl-Cl giving two H-Cl), the bonds to be broken circled on the left with their energies, the bonds made circled on the right with their energies. Under it a ladder: an upward arrow for the energy in, a longer downward arrow for the energy out, and a vertical arrow for the overall change.
params: reaction (H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl | CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O | H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr | N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3), bond energy values (given), show the working (boolean)
scienceChecks: The bonds broken are counted from the reactants times their coefficients and the bonds made from the products. Energy change = bonds broken minus bonds made. A negative result is exothermic and a positive result endothermic. Atoms are balanced on both sides.
notes: Higher Tier. AQA exam questions give a displayed-formula equation and a bond energy table.

name: Temperature change of a reaction in a polystyrene cup (required practical)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the temperatureChange template: a polystyrene cup with a lid in a beaker, a thermometer through the lid hole, the solution at about 50 percent. Label cup, lid, thermometer, beaker.
params: contents (acid and alkali), lid on or off
scienceChecks: The thermometer bulb is in the liquid and not on the base. The cup stands in the beaker, which stops it tipping. The lid has a hole for the thermometer.
notes: Required practical 4 of 8462 and 10 of Trilogy.

name: Simple cell: two metals in an electrolyte with a voltmeter
subject: chemistry
draw: A beaker of electrolyte (Colourless solution) with two different metal strips (the electrode symbol, metal strip) standing in it without touching each other. Wires from the tops of the strips to a voltmeter (meter box titled voltmeter, two terminals). Labels give the two metals, the electrolyte and the voltmeter. Optional plus and minus signs on the strips.
params: metal 1, metal 2 (magnesium | zinc | iron | copper), electrolyte, meter reading (text)
scienceChecks: The two metals are different (identical metals give no voltage). The strips do not touch. Both dip into the electrolyte. The meter is in the circuit. The more reactive metal is the negative terminal. The voltage is larger for metals further apart in the reactivity series.
notes: Chemistry only in 8462. A new template from existing symbols. The existing electrochemicalCell template has a salt bridge and two beakers, which is the A-level version.

name: Hydrogen fuel cell
subject: chemistry
draw: A box with an electrolyte in the middle and a porous electrode on each side. Hydrogen enters at the left electrode (negative), oxygen or air at the right (positive), and water leaves at the right. An outside circuit with a bulb or motor joins the electrodes, with arrows for the flow of electrons from the negative electrode to the positive electrode. For an acid electrolyte, hydrogen ions cross the electrolyte. Labels on every part. Option: half-equations beside each electrode (Higher Tier).
params: electrolyte (acid | alkaline), show half-equations (boolean), show electron arrows (boolean), load (bulb | motor)
scienceChecks: Hydrogen enters at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive one. Electrons flow in the outside wire from the negative to the positive electrode. The only product is water. Half-equations balance for atoms and charge: 2H2 -> 4H+ + 4e-, O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O, overall 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
notes: Chemistry only in 8462. The half-equation forms shown are the usual acid forms; AQA's own forms were not visible in the text I read, so check them.

name: Temperature against time or volume for a reaction
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes with scales, plotted points and a line of best fit, for the temperature change against the volume of alkali added, or against time. Students read the maximum temperature change from it.
params: x quantity, data points, line of best fit
scienceChecks: The maximum temperature change is read at the top of the best-fit lines; the lines for neutralisation meet at a peak.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. From memory of the practical.

name: Rate graph: amount of product against time, with a tangent
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Axes with scales: time along the bottom, volume of gas (or mass of product, or mass lost) up the side. One to three curves that start at the origin, rise steeply and flatten to a plateau. For Higher Tier a straight tangent drawn on a curve at a stated time, with the gradient triangle. Curves for a faster reaction start steeper and reach the same plateau.
params: curves (1 to 3), quantity on the vertical axis (gas volume | product mass | mass lost), tangent at time t (boolean), labels for the conditions
scienceChecks: Every curve starts at the origin and its gradient falls to zero. For the same amount of limiting reactant all curves reach the same plateau, and a catalyst does not change the plateau. A faster reaction has a steeper start. The tangent touches the curve at one point and its gradient equals the rate at that time.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. AQA asks students to draw tangents and, at Higher Tier, to find the gradient. Priority A is how often it is drawn in lessons and papers; it is not a build order.

name: Rate of reaction: gas collected in a gas syringe
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Use the rateGasSyringe template: a conical flask of acid with marble chips and bubbles, a bung and a tube to a gas syringe held by a clamp, a stopwatch beside the stand. Label flask, acid, marble chips, gas syringe, stopwatch.
params: acid concentration label, syringe plunger position
scienceChecks: The flask is sealed apart from the tube to the syringe (S13). The syringe is held horizontally by a clamp. The plunger position shows a volume between 0 and the syringe capacity.
notes: Required practical 5 of 8462 (11 of Trilogy). AQA says a gas syringe can replace the trough and cylinder.

name: Rate of reaction: gas collected over water
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Use the rateGasOverWater template: a flask of acid with magnesium ribbon, a one-hole bung and delivery tube to a trough of water, an upside-down measuring cylinder full of water held by a clamp over the tube end, a stopwatch. Label flask, bung, delivery tube, trough, measuring cylinder.
params: gas volume in the cylinder, acid label
scienceChecks: The delivery tube end is under the open mouth of the cylinder. The cylinder mouth is below the water surface. The only opening of the flask system is the water in the trough (S13).
notes: Required practical 5 of 8462 (11 of Trilogy).

name: Rate of reaction: disappearing cross (sodium thiosulfate and acid)
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Use the disappearingCross template: a flask on a paper with a cross, the observer looking down into the flask, a stopwatch, a thermometer in the cloudy yellow mixture. Label the cross, the flask, the observer and the stopwatch.
params: mixture cloudiness, thermometer on or off
scienceChecks: The cross is under the flask and visible from above. The observer looks through the top of the flask. The mixture is cloudy when the cross has just gone.
notes: Required practical 5 of 8462 (11 of Trilogy) and A-level practical 3.

name: Collision theory: particle pictures for concentration, temperature and surface area
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Pairs of boxes with a short caption. Concentration or pressure: the same volume with few particles and with many. Temperature: the same particles with short and with long movement arrows. Surface area: a block and the same block cut into small pieces, with exposed faces marked. A starburst marks each collision where two particles touch. A caption such as 'more collisions in each second' under the second box.
params: factor (concentration | pressure | temperature | surface area | catalyst), particles in each box (4 to 30), show collision marks (boolean), show arrows (boolean)
scienceChecks: A concentration or pressure pair has equal box volumes and different particle counts. A temperature pair has equal counts and longer arrows in the hot box. A surface area pair has equal total volume of solid. A collision mark appears only where two particles touch.
notes: Reuses the particle box and the cube pictures.

name: Reversible reaction reaching equilibrium in a closed container
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Three sealed boxes in a row: at the start (all reactant particles), part-way, and at equilibrium. Between them a pair of arrows labelled forward and backward, the two arrows equal in length at equilibrium. A closed lid on each box. Reactant and product particles differ by shape and fill. Optional equation with the reversible arrow under the boxes.
params: reaction (A to B | N2O4 and NO2 | H2 and I2 and HI), particles (6 to 24), stage labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: Atoms are conserved in every box. The particle counts of each kind are the same in the last two boxes. At equilibrium the forward and backward arrows are drawn equal. The box is closed.
notes: AQA defines equilibrium as equal forward and reverse rates in a closed system. The picture form is a teaching convention.

name: Concentration against time as a reaction reaches equilibrium
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Axes: concentration up, time along. A falling curve for the reactant and a rising curve for the product that both level off, from time zero, with a vertical dashed line where equilibrium starts. Used at A-level for a change in conditions (a step in a curve).
params: reaction, initial concentrations, time of a disturbance (optional), which curve is blank
scienceChecks: Concentrations stop changing together. The reactant fall equals the product rise in moles for a 1 to 1 reaction. After a disturbance, the curves re-level at new values.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. Also used at A-level.

name: Nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide in a sealed syringe (pressure change)
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Two gas syringes side by side. The first holds a brown gas (Brown gas preset). In the second the plunger is pushed in, the volume is smaller, and the brown colour is at first darker then fades to a paler brown as the equilibrium shifts to the colourless N2O4. Labels: brown NO2, colourless N2O4, plunger pushed in.
params: plunger position, gas colour, before or after the shift
scienceChecks: The pushed-in syringe has a smaller volume. The final colour is paler than the first moment after compressing, because the equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules. Equation 2NO2 reacting reversibly to N2O4 is balanced.
notes: The sealed-syringe question for pressure changes was reported in the AQA search summary; Higher Tier idea.

name: Heating hydrated copper sulfate (a reversible reaction)
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: A boiling tube held by a test-tube holder (or a clamp) at a slope with its mouth lower than its closed end, blue crystals (Blue crystals preset) at the closed end, a Bunsen with a blue flame under the crystals, water droplets near the mouth. A second picture: the white powder with a few drops of water added from a dropper, turning blue again.
params: stage (heating | adding water), tube holder or clamp
scienceChecks: The tube is open (the mouth faces slightly down so condensed water runs out, not back onto hot glass). The flame is at the crystals. The after-heating powder is white and the re-hydrated powder is blue.
notes: From memory of the standard demonstration. Whether AQA names this example was not confirmed in the text I read.

name: Graphs of ammonia yield against pressure and temperature
subject: chemistry
topic: The rate and extent of chemical change
draw: Axes: percentage yield of ammonia up, pressure along, with three curves for three temperatures (the lowest temperature on top). A mark at the conditions used in industry. Higher Tier students read the graph and explain the compromise between rate and yield.
params: temperatures shown (3), industrial point marked (boolean)
scienceChecks: Yield rises with pressure at a fixed temperature. Yield is lower at higher temperature for the exothermic forward reaction. Curves do not cross.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. Higher Tier; the AQA search summary names graphs of conditions in this section.

name: Fractional distillation of crude oil (industrial column)
subject: chemistry
draw: A tall column drawn as a vertical rectangle with horizontal trays, hot at the bottom and cool at the top (a temperature arrow). Crude oil is heated in a furnace and the vapour enters near the bottom. Pipes on the right take off fractions at different heights: refinery gases at the top, then petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil, and bitumen at the bottom. Beside the pipes, arrows for the trends: boiling point, chain length and viscosity increase downwards; flammability increases upwards.
params: fractions shown (5 to 7), show chain lengths (boolean), show trend arrows (boolean), show furnace (boolean), blank labels for a worksheet (boolean)
scienceChecks: Fractions with longer chains and higher boiling points leave lower down. The vapour enters near the bottom. The top is cooler than the bottom. Carbon ranges increase downwards (gases about 1 to 4, petrol next, then kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen).
notes: AQA asks students to explain the separation using the temperature gradient; examiners reported that students who referred to a labelled diagram gained from it. Carbon number ranges differ between sources, so they are parameters.

name: Displayed formula of an alkane or alkene
subject: chemistry
draw: C and H in 15 u text joined by single lines, a double line for C=C. A straight chain of carbons with hydrogens above and below, bonds at right angles, lines long enough to read. Optional ring versions drawn as a polygon with the C atoms at the corners, since cyclohexene appears in exam questions. Name and molecular formula beside it when asked.
params: family (alkane | alkene | cycloalkane | cycloalkene), carbons (1 to 8), double bond position, show molecular formula (boolean), show name (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each carbon has four bonds, counting a double bond as two. Molecular formulae: alkane CnH(2n+2), alkene and cycloalkane CnH2n, cycloalkene CnH(2n-2). An alkene has at least two carbons. The name stem matches the carbon count (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct).
notes: AQA asks for fully displayed formulae of the first four alkenes. The same engine serves A-level, which adds skeletal formulae.

name: Displayed formula of an alcohol or a carboxylic acid
subject: chemistry
draw: A straight carbon chain with hydrogens, plus the functional group drawn in full: -O-H for an alcohol, -C(=O)-O-H for a carboxylic acid, with every bond shown. The functional group can be circled when the question asks the student to circle it. Name and molecular formula beside it when asked.
params: family (alcohol | carboxylic acid), carbons (1 to 5), circle the functional group (boolean), show name (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each C has four bonds, each O two and each H one. Molecular formulae: alcohol CnH(2n+1)OH, acid CnH(2n+1)COOH (counting the carboxyl carbon in n+1). The carboxyl carbon has one C=O and one O-H.
notes: Chemistry only in 8462 (4.7.2). AQA asks students to complete a part-drawn ethanol formula and to circle an alcohol group.

name: Ester formation (alcohol plus carboxylic acid) in displayed formulae
subject: chemistry
draw: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol as displayed formulae joined by a plus sign, a reaction arrow, and the ester with the new C-O-C link in the middle and water as the second product. The ester link -COO- is circled on request. Example: ethanoic acid and ethanol giving ethyl ethanoate.
params: acid (methanoic | ethanoic | propanoic), alcohol (methanol | ethanol | propanol), circle the ester link (boolean)
scienceChecks: Atoms are conserved: the ester plus water have the same atoms as the acid plus alcohol. The ester has one C=O and one C-O-C link. The ester name is alcohol-stem then acid-stem 'oate'.
notes: AQA asks which displayed formula is the ester from ethanoic acid and ethanol.

name: Addition reactions of alkenes (hydrogen, water, halogens) in displayed formulae
subject: chemistry
draw: The alkene as a displayed formula, a plus sign and the reagent (H-H, H-O-H, Cl-Cl, Br-Br, I-I), an arrow, and the product with the double bond now single and the new atoms on the two carbons. The two carbons that gained atoms are marked. A small label gives the condition or the observation (bromine water going from orange to colourless).
params: alkene (ethene | propene | butene | pentene), reagent (H2 | H2O | Cl2 | Br2 | I2), show the condition label (boolean)
scienceChecks: Atoms are conserved. The product has no C=C. Each of the two carbons of the double bond gains one atom or group. Addition of water gives an alcohol and addition of a halogen gives a dihaloalkane.
notes: Chemistry only in 8462 (4.7.2). AQA asks for the first four alkenes and these five reagents.

name: Addition polymerisation (monomer to repeating unit)
subject: chemistry
draw: The monomer as a displayed formula (with C=C), an arrow labelled with n and the catalyst or conditions, and the polymer drawn as the repeating unit inside square brackets with the bonds running out through the brackets and a subscript n. An alternative picture draws three repeat units in a row. Monomers: ethene, propene, chloroethene, tetrafluoroethene, styrene.
params: monomer (ethene | propene | chloroethene | tetrafluoroethene | styrene), show repeating unit in brackets with n (boolean), show three units (boolean)
scienceChecks: The repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer. The C=C of the monomer is a single C-C in the polymer. Side groups are unchanged. The bonds cross the square brackets and n is shown.
notes: Chemistry only in 8462 (4.7.3). AQA asks students to draw the formation from a given alkene and to relate the repeat unit to the monomer.

name: Condensation polymerisation (diol and dicarboxylic acid) with block diagrams
subject: chemistry
draw: Two monomers drawn as a rectangle (the carbon chain) with the functional groups at the two ends drawn in full: HO-OC- ... -CO-OH for the acid and H-O- ... -O-H for the diol. A reaction arrow, then a chain section with the ester links formed and a small water molecule leaving at each link. The repeating unit is bracketed.
params: monomer pair (diol and dicarboxylic acid | diamine and dicarboxylic acid | amino acid), blocks as boxes or as skeletal chains, show water leaving (boolean)
scienceChecks: One water molecule leaves at each link formed. The repeating unit alternates the two blocks. Atoms are conserved including the water. The links are ester, amide or peptide as the pair determines.
notes: Higher Tier in 8462 (4.7.3.2). AQA exam questions ask for the small molecule lost (water) in a table.

name: Amino acid and dipeptide in displayed formulae
subject: chemistry
draw: The general amino acid H2N-CH(R)-COOH in displayed formula, with the amine and carboxyl groups marked, and glycine as the example (R is H). Optional: two amino acids joined, with the peptide link drawn and a water molecule leaving.
params: amino acid (general | glycine | alanine), show dipeptide formation (boolean), mark the functional groups (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each amino acid has one amine and one carboxyl group (two functional groups). Forming a peptide link loses one H2O. Atoms of C, H, N and O are conserved.
notes: Higher Tier chemistry only in 8462. AQA asks how many functional groups glycine has.

name: DNA: double helix, nucleotide and base pairs
subject: chemistry
draw: Two ribbons twisted round each other with rungs for the base pairs, and one nucleotide in detail: a circle for the phosphate, a pentagon for the sugar and a rectangle for the base, joined in a line. The four bases are named (A, T, C, G) and the pairs shown (A with T, C with G). Arrows show the two strands running in opposite directions.
params: view (double helix | ladder | single nucleotide), show base names (boolean), show the pairing (boolean)
scienceChecks: A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Each nucleotide has one phosphate, one sugar and one base. The two strands are antiparallel. The counts of A and T are equal, and of C and G are equal.
notes: AQA examiners reported that students recognised the double helix but seldom mentioned four monomers or two chains. The same picture is needed in biology.

name: Natural polymers as chains of monomers (starch, cellulose, protein)
subject: chemistry
draw: A chain of repeated boxes or circles (glucose units for starch and cellulose, amino acids for a protein) joined end to end, with the repeating unit bracketed. A pair of chains side by side for cellulose, a coiled chain for starch.
params: polymer (starch | cellulose | protein), units (4 to 10), show the repeating unit (boolean)
scienceChecks: Units are joined end to end with no branching in the simple version. The monomer type matches the polymer.
notes: The AQA text names these polymers; the picture is a block chain from memory.

name: Laboratory cracking of a hydrocarbon
subject: chemistry
draw: A boiling tube lying almost horizontal and held by a clamp, with mineral wool soaked in paraffin at the closed end and pieces of catalyst (broken porcelain or aluminium oxide, a Chips layer) in the middle, heated strongly by a Bunsen. A bung and a delivery tube lead to a trough of water, with a test tube filled with water upside down over the end to collect the gas. A label says to take the delivery tube out of the water before stopping the heating.
params: collect gas over water (boolean), second tube of bromine water for the test (boolean)
scienceChecks: The paraffin wool is at the closed end and the catalyst in the strongly heated part. The delivery tube end is under the inverted full test tube. The only opening is the trough (S13). The collected gas turns bromine water colourless.
notes: A new template from existing symbols (boilingTube, clampStand, bossClamp, bunsenBurner, bung, trough, testTube, cottonWool). The AQA text I read asks for cracking conditions and equations, not this apparatus, so priority is B.

name: Cracking drawn as a long molecule breaking into smaller ones
subject: chemistry
draw: A long-chain alkane as a displayed formula (for example decane), a reaction arrow labelled with the catalyst or steam and high temperature, and the products: a shorter alkane and one or more alkenes, drawn as displayed formulae. A mark across one C-C bond of the reactant shows where it breaks.
params: reactant (C8H18 | C10H22 | C12H26), products chosen, mark the break (boolean)
scienceChecks: The numbers of C and H atoms are equal on both sides. Each alkene product is CnH2n and each alkane is CnH(2n+2). At least one product is an alkene.
notes: AQA asks students to balance cracking equations from formulae; the displayed version is a teaching extension.

name: Fermentation of a sugar solution (apparatus)
subject: chemistry
draw: A conical flask of sugar solution and yeast closed with a bung and a delivery tube that dips into limewater in a test tube, with the flask standing in a beaker of warm water (about 35 degrees) and a thermometer in the water bath. Bubbles in the flask and in the limewater, which turns cloudy.
params: limewater test tube (boolean), water bath (boolean), airlock instead of limewater (boolean)
scienceChecks: The flask is closed except for the delivery tube (anaerobic, S13). The delivery tube dips below the limewater surface. The bath temperature is in the warm range, not boiling.
notes: AQA names fermentation with yeast at warm temperatures in 4.7.2.3 (chemistry only); the apparatus is a classroom choice and is from memory.

name: Testing the products of burning a hydrocarbon fuel
subject: chemistry
draw: A spirit burner or candle under a funnel, a tube from the funnel to a U-tube standing in a beaker of ice (liquid collects), a second tube to a test tube of limewater (turns cloudy), and a tube to a filter pump that draws the gases through. Labels: fuel, ice, condensate, limewater, to pump.
params: fuel (ethanol burner | candle), show the cobalt chloride paper test (boolean)
scienceChecks: Gases are drawn through the ice-cooled tube before the limewater. The limewater tube inlet dips under the surface. The system is open only at the funnel and the pump (S13).
notes: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water (the AQA text). The apparatus is a standard teaching one from memory; many schools show the result as a table.

name: Bromine water test for an alkene
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the testTubeReactions template with two tubes in a rack: bromine water (Orange preset) with an alkane, which stays orange; and with an alkene, which goes colourless (Colourless solution preset). Labels say which is which. A dropper above the tubes.
params: hydrocarbon in each tube (alkane | alkene), before or after
scienceChecks: The alkene tube is colourless after shaking and the alkane tube stays orange. The colour change is written as orange to colourless, never to clear.
notes: AQA asks students to recall the colour change.

name: From crude oil to polymers (fractional distillation, cracking, polymerisation)
subject: chemistry
draw: Boxes joined by arrows: crude oil, fractional distillation, long-chain fractions, cracking, alkenes and shorter alkanes, polymerisation, polymers. Each arrow is labelled with the process. An exam mark scheme lists these three stages in order.
params: label mode (names | blank for a worksheet)
scienceChecks: The stages run in the order distillation, cracking, polymerisation. Cracking takes long-chain fractions and gives alkenes.
notes: An AQA mark scheme for a question on this sequence was reported through the search tool; no AQA flow diagram was seen, so the row is from memory.

name: Paper chromatogram with Rf measurements
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the chromatography paper symbol, developed: a pencil start line near the bottom, several spots (a pure substance gives one spot, a mixture several) and the solvent front line near the top. Add two dimension lines (a line with tick end caps) parallel to the edge: from the start line to the centre of one spot, and from the start line to the solvent front, each with its length in millimetres. Beside it, Rf = distance moved by the spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent.
params: spots (1 to 6), front position, developed (boolean), distances shown (boolean), known samples beside the unknown
scienceChecks: Distances are measured from the start line, to the centre of a spot and to the solvent front. Rf is between 0 and 1. A spot cannot be above the solvent front. A pure substance gives one spot. The measuring lines are parallel to the paper edge.
notes: AQA asks students to read distances from a chromatogram figure and calculate Rf. Required practical 6 of 8462 (12 of Trilogy).

name: Paper chromatography apparatus
subject: chemistry
