draw: Use the paperChromatography template: a beaker with a little solvent, a paper hanging from a rod across the rim, the pencil start line above the solvent level, and the spots on the line. Add a watch glass or lid on the beaker when the question asks for the lid. Label beaker, solvent, pencil line, paper.
params: solvent level, lid on or off, spots
scienceChecks: The start line is in pencil and above the solvent surface. The paper does not touch the beaker wall. The beaker has a lid in the corrected version. The solvent level is below the start line.
notes: An AQA question shows a chromatography set-up with two mistakes (the lid and the start line were the common answers). Required practical 6.

name: Filtration apparatus (separating an insoluble solid)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the filtration template: a funnel with fluted or folded filter paper standing in the neck of a conical flask, the residue (for example sand) on the paper and the filtrate in the flask. Label funnel, filter paper, residue, filtrate.
params: residue (boolean), filtrate level, label mode
scienceChecks: The funnel stem is inside the flask mouth. The paper sits inside the funnel and below its rim. The residue is on the paper and the filtrate below.
notes: An AQA past paper asked students to draw filtration apparatus and label where the sand is collected. Also used in preparing a salt.

name: Tests for hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and chlorine
subject: chemistry
draw: Four small pictures. Hydrogen: a lit splint at the mouth of a test tube of gas (squeaky pop). Oxygen: a glowing splint going into a test tube of gas, relighting. Carbon dioxide: gas bubbled through limewater in a test tube, which goes cloudy. Chlorine: damp litmus paper held at the mouth of a test tube of pale green gas, bleached white. Each picture has a one-line result under it.
params: gas (hydrogen | oxygen | carbon dioxide | chlorine | ammonia), show the result label (boolean), blank result for a worksheet
scienceChecks: Hydrogen uses a lit splint, oxygen a glowing splint, chlorine damp (not dry) litmus paper, carbon dioxide limewater. The result label matches the gas: squeaky pop, relights, goes cloudy, bleaches. The splint is at the mouth of the tube, not in a liquid.
notes: A new template group from existing symbols (testTube, splint, indicatorPaper, testTubeRack, glass tube). Gas tests are in 4.8.2 for both courses.

name: Test for a carbonate (acid, then limewater)
subject: chemistry
draw: A test tube of the solid carbonate with dilute acid added from a dropper, fizzing, closed with a bung and a delivery tube that dips into limewater in a second test tube, which turns cloudy. Both tubes in a rack or clamp. Labels: carbonate, acid, delivery tube, limewater.
params: carbonate (calcium carbonate | copper carbonate | sodium carbonate), limewater state (clear | cloudy)
scienceChecks: The delivery tube end dips below the limewater surface. The first tube is closed by the bung with the delivery tube as the only opening (S13). Bubbles appear in the first tube. The limewater is cloudy after the test.
notes: Chemistry only. AQA: add acid to the carbonate and test the gas with limewater. The new template reuses the delivery-tube-into-limewater layout of thermalDecomposition, without the heating.

name: Flame test apparatus (nichrome wire in a blue flame)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the flameTest template: a Bunsen burner on a heatproof mat with a blue flame, and a nichrome wire loop held in the edge of the flame. Add a test tube of dilute acid beside it for cleaning the wire. Labels: nichrome wire, blue flame, sample, acid for cleaning.
params: flame (blue), sample label, acid tube (boolean)
scienceChecks: The flame is blue (air hole open). The loop is in the edge of the flame. The wire is cleaned in acid between samples.
notes: Required practical 7 of 8462 (chemistry only). AQA reported that students forgot the cleaning step.

name: Flame test colours (lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, copper)
subject: chemistry
draw: Five Bunsen flames side by side, each with the flame colour of one metal ion and the name below: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green. Colours are test colours (S6). Each flame also has its colour written under it so that the picture survives photocopying.
params: ions shown (Li+ | Na+ | K+ | Ca2+ | Cu2+), label mode (names | blank)
scienceChecks: The colour matches the ion: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green. A flame with a mixture of ions can hide colours.
notes: This is a small change to the existing flame and bunsenBurner symbols (a tint parameter), not a new symbol.

name: Halide and sulfate precipitate tests in test tubes
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the testTubeReactions template with four tubes. Halides: add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate; chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide a cream one, iodide a yellow one (the Cream and Yellow presets). Sulfate: add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride; a white precipitate. Labels give the reagents and the colour.
params: ion in each tube, reagents, precipitate preset
scienceChecks: Chloride is white, bromide cream, iodide yellow with silver nitrate. Sulfate gives a white precipitate with barium chloride. The acid is added before the test reagent.
notes: AQA notes that cream and yellow are hard to tell apart, so the practical suggests comparing side by side. Chemistry only.

name: Metal hydroxide precipitates with sodium hydroxide solution
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the testTubeReactions template with six tubes: aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions give white precipitates (aluminium dissolving in excess alkali), copper(II) gives a blue precipitate, iron(II) a green one, iron(III) a brown one. Labels give the ion and the colour. A dropper above the tubes.
params: ion in each tube, excess alkali (boolean)
scienceChecks: Copper(II) is blue, iron(II) green, iron(III) brown, and the other three white. Only aluminium dissolves in excess. The precipitate settles at the bottom of the tube.
notes: From memory: the AQA summary I read did not retrieve the metal hydroxide wording. There is no pale green precipitate preset; the green powder preset is close.

name: Flame emission spectra (known ions and a mixture)
subject: chemistry
draw: Strips of line spectra on a common wavelength scale: one strip for each known metal ion and one for the unknown mixture, each a dark background with bright vertical lines at fixed positions. Students match the lines in the mixture with the reference strips.
params: ions (Li+ | Na+ | K+ | Ca2+ | Cu2+), mixture of two or three (boolean), wavelength axis (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every line of the mixture appears in a reference strip. The lines of one ion are at the same wavelength in every strip where it is present. The wavelength axis is the same for every strip.
notes: Spectrum: outside PracDraw unless James brings spectra into scope. A 2018 specimen question gives five reference spectra and a mixture. Chemistry only.

name: Flow chart for identifying an unknown ionic compound
subject: chemistry
draw: A flow chart of tests with boxes and yes/no arrows: flame test, then sodium hydroxide, then the acid tests for carbonate, halide and sulfate, ending in the ions identified. A student completes it from observations.
params: which branches are filled, blank boxes
scienceChecks: Each test result leads to exactly one next box. The end boxes name ions consistent with the tests on the path.
notes: A generic decision-tree drawing. Whether AQA uses this exact chart was not seen.

name: Water analysis and purification (distillation set-up)
subject: chemistry
draw: Use the simpleDistillation template: a conical flask of salty water on a gauze over a Bunsen burner, a two-hole bung with a thermometer and a delivery tube to a test tube standing in a beaker of ice and water. For the dissolved-solids test add the crystallisation picture (an evaporating basin heated over a beaker). For the pH test a beaker with a pH probe or indicator paper.
params: sample colour, thermometer on or off, ice bath
scienceChecks: The flask is open only through the delivery tube, whose end is above the collected liquid (S13). The thermometer bulb is level with the delivery-tube inlet, not in the liquid. The collecting tube stands in ice.
notes: Required practical 8 of 8462 (13 of Trilogy). The template covers the distillation; the pH and dissolved-solids tests need the crystallisation picture and a pH probe in a beaker.

name: Composition of dry air (pie chart, bar chart or particle grid)
subject: chemistry
draw: A pie chart or bar chart of the gases in dry air: nitrogen about 78 percent, oxygen about 21 percent, argon about 1 percent, carbon dioxide about 0.04 percent. Alternative: a 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares, 78 marked nitrogen, 21 oxygen, 1 argon, labelled with a key. Slices carry their names and numbers.
params: style (pie | bar | grid), show values (boolean), compare with another planet (boolean)
scienceChecks: The percentages sum to 100. Nitrogen is the largest and oxygen about a quarter of the nitrogen slice. Carbon dioxide is too small to see on a pie chart, and the picture says so.
notes: Chart: outside PracDraw unless James brings charts into scope. The grid version is a particle-style picture that PracDraw could draw as a symbol.

name: How the gases in the atmosphere changed over time
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes: percentage of gas up the side, time since the Earth formed along the bottom. A falling curve for carbon dioxide, a rising curve for oxygen and a rising curve for nitrogen, with regions A, B and C marked along the bottom for the students to explain.
params: gases shown, regions marked (boolean), time scale labels
scienceChecks: Carbon dioxide falls as oxygen rises. Nitrogen rises to its present level and stays. Percentages never exceed 100 together.
notes: Chart: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. AQA papers show a graph with regions A, B and C and ask what caused each change.

name: The greenhouse effect
subject: chemistry
draw: The Sun at the top, the Earth's surface at the bottom and a band for the atmosphere across the middle. Arrows: short-wave radiation from the Sun passing through the atmosphere to the surface; long-wave (infrared) radiation leaving the surface upwards; part of it absorbed by the greenhouse gases in the band and re-emitted in all directions, some back down to the surface, some out to space. Labels: carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour; the temperature of the surface rising. A second panel with more greenhouse gas has a thicker band and more arrows returning.
params: panels (normal | enhanced | both), label mode (names | blank), show gas names (boolean)
scienceChecks: Incoming arrows are labelled short-wave and outgoing arrows long-wave (infrared). Some outgoing radiation is returned to the surface, and the enhanced panel returns more than the normal one. Nothing passes from the atmosphere to the Sun.
notes: The AQA wording that asks students to draw the greenhouse effect was seen in a Combined Science (possibly Synergy) page, not in the 8462 text, so the row is secondary. Revision sites differ on the incoming radiation (ultraviolet or short-wave).

name: Carbon cycle (simple, for the atmosphere topic)
subject: chemistry
draw: Boxes for the atmosphere (carbon dioxide), plants and algae, animals, decomposers, fossil fuels, and oceans and rocks, joined by arrows labelled photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decay, combustion, formation of fossil fuels, dissolving. The atmosphere box is at the centre.
params: label mode (names | blank for a worksheet), extra arrows for burning fossil fuels (boolean)
scienceChecks: Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere into plants. Respiration, decay and combustion put it back. Every arrow joins the correct two boxes. Fossil fuels form from dead organisms.
notes: Mostly a biology (ecology) picture; a chemistry version links to the early atmosphere and fossil fuels. One shared drawing for the two subjects.

name: Carbon dioxide concentration and global temperature against time
subject: chemistry
draw: One or two line graphs with years along the bottom: carbon dioxide concentration (parts per million) rising, and average global surface temperature rising, on separate axes one above the other. Students calculate a percentage increase and judge whether a correlation shows a cause.
params: years, quantities, one or two graphs
scienceChecks: The two graphs share the same time axis. Both curves rise over the period. The percentage increase equals (final minus first) divided by first.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. Several AQA papers use dual graphs of this kind.

name: How acid rain forms and what it damages
subject: chemistry
draw: A power station or car on the left burning a fuel, with sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen rising into a cloud; the gases dissolve in water droplets; rain falls on a limestone building, a lake and trees. Each arrow is labelled with the change (sulfur dioxide from sulfur in fuel, nitrogen oxides from nitrogen and oxygen at a high temperature, dissolving to make acid).
params: pollutant (sulfur dioxide | oxides of nitrogen | both), show damage (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: Sulfur dioxide comes from fuels that contain sulfur. Oxides of nitrogen come from nitrogen and oxygen in air at high temperature. The product is dilute sulfuric or nitric acid. Limestone (calcium carbonate) is the material damaged.

name: Catalytic converter (cross-section)
subject: chemistry
draw: A tube cut away to show a honeycomb ceramic block coated with a metal catalyst, exhaust gases entering on the left (carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen, unburnt hydrocarbons) and cleaner gases leaving on the right (carbon dioxide, nitrogen, water). Arrows and labels only.
params: label mode, show equations (boolean)
scienceChecks: Atoms of C, N and O are conserved between the gases entering and leaving. The product gases are carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water.
notes: Nice-to-have. I did not see this picture in the AQA text; it is used in teaching of atmospheric pollutants.

name: Treatment of water to make it safe to drink (potable water)
subject: chemistry
draw: A flow diagram from left to right: a fresh water source (a reservoir or river), screening to remove large objects, a settling tank (sedimentation), filter beds of sand and gravel, then sterilising with chlorine (or ozone or ultraviolet light), then a storage tower and supply. Each stage is a labelled box with an arrow, and a short note on what it removes: large objects, solids, microbes.
params: stages shown (3 to 6), sterilising method (chlorine | ozone | ultraviolet), label mode (names | blank)
scienceChecks: Sterilising comes after filtration. The stages run in the order source, screen, settle, filter, sterilise. Every box joins the next with one arrow.
notes: AQA describes the sequence as choosing a source, filter beds, then sterilising. Exam questions give the stages and ask students to sort or complete them.

name: Desalination by reverse osmosis
subject: chemistry
draw: Salt water enters on the left, passes a high-pressure pump and meets a membrane drawn as a dashed barrier across a pipe. Fresh water leaves on one side of the membrane and a more concentrated salt solution (brine) leaves on the other. Optional particle dots: salt ions held back, water molecules passing through. A label says the process needs a lot of energy.
params: show particles (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: Only water passes the membrane. The brine is more concentrated than the feed. The pressure is applied on the salt-water side.
notes: Desalination by distillation is covered by the waterAnalysisPurification row (the simpleDistillation template).

name: Treatment of waste water (sewage)
subject: chemistry
draw: A flow chart with two branches. Raw sewage goes to screening and grit removal, then to sedimentation. The settled sewage sludge goes down one branch to anaerobic digestion; the liquid effluent goes along the other to aerobic biological treatment, then is released. Each box labelled, with arrows.
params: label mode (names | blank for matching), show gas from digestion (boolean)
scienceChecks: Sedimentation produces sludge and effluent. Sludge goes to anaerobic digestion and effluent to aerobic treatment. Screening and grit removal come first. No box has two outgoing arrows except sedimentation.
notes: Chemistry only. AQA exam questions ask students to complete this flow chart or to match substances to treatments.

name: Phytomining flow diagram
subject: chemistry
draw: Boxes and arrows: plants grown on soil with a low metal content, the plants absorb metal compounds, the plants are harvested, burned, giving ash that contains metal compounds, and the metal is extracted from the ash (by displacement or by electrolysis). A small plant icon in the first box.
params: label mode, show extraction methods (boolean)
scienceChecks: Burning follows harvesting. The ash holds metal compounds. The final step is a displacement or an electrolysis.
notes: Chemistry only. Examiners reported that students confused phytomining with bioleaching.

name: Bioleaching flow diagram
subject: chemistry
draw: Boxes and arrows: low-grade copper ore, bacteria added, a leachate solution containing metal compounds is produced, and the metal is extracted from the leachate (displacement or electrolysis). A small bacteria icon.
params: label mode, show extraction methods (boolean)
scienceChecks: The leachate is a solution of copper compounds, not copper itself. The bacteria act on the ore. The final step is a displacement or an electrolysis.
notes: Chemistry only. The two boxes are drawn with the same pattern as phytomining so students can compare them.

name: Life cycle assessment (stages of a product's life)
subject: chemistry
draw: A cycle or a row of four boxes: extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use and operation during the lifetime, disposal at the end of life (with recycling feeding back to the first box). Each box has space for a note or a number for energy, water, waste and carbon dioxide.
params: product label, show recycling arrow (boolean), show data boxes (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: There are four stages in this order. Recycling returns to the raw materials or manufacturing stage. Data boxes for different products use the same units.
notes: AQA exam questions mostly give the data as a table (see lcaTable).

name: Table of life cycle assessment data (two products)
subject: chemistry
draw: A table with columns for two products (for example a plastic bag and a paper bag) and rows for energy, water, waste and carbon dioxide at each stage. Students compare and evaluate.
params: products, stages, which cells are blank
scienceChecks: Units are consistent within a row. Totals equal the sums of the stages.
notes: Table: outside PracDraw unless James brings tables into scope.

name: Recycling loop for metals, glass or plastics
subject: chemistry
draw: A loop of boxes: collect, sort, melt or reprocess, manufacture a new product, use, collect again. Arrows labelled with energy saved against extraction from ore.
params: material (metal | glass | plastic), label mode
scienceChecks: The loop returns to collection. Recycling uses less energy than extraction (a label, not a number).
notes: Nice-to-have, from memory.

name: Rusting experiment (nails in test tubes)
subject: chemistry
draw: Four test tubes in a rack, each with an iron nail. Tube 1: tap water, open to air (the nail rusts, drawn with brown marks). Tube 2: boiled water with a layer of oil on top (no oxygen, no rust). Tube 3: anhydrous calcium chloride and a bung (no water, no rust). Tube 4: salt solution (rusts faster). Labels say what is in each tube and the result.
params: tubes shown (3 or 4), result marks (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: Rust appears only where both water and oxygen are present. Tube 2 has oil above boiled water. Tube 3 is closed with a bung and holds a drying agent. Each nail is fully inside its tube.
notes: Chemistry only (4.10.3). A new template from existing symbols; there is no nail symbol, so a metal electrode rod stands in. A nail symbol would help here and in the displacement rows.

name: Sacrificial protection and galvanising
subject: chemistry
draw: Sacrificial protection: part of a steel hull or pipe with a block of zinc (or magnesium) attached by a metal contact and an arrow showing the zinc dissolving instead of the iron. Galvanising: a cross-section of iron with a layer of zinc on top, a scratch down to the iron, and a note that the zinc still protects. A comparison with a tin coating, where the barrier fails when scratched, is optional.
params: mode (sacrificial block | galvanised coating | tin coating), show electron flow (boolean)
scienceChecks: The protecting metal is more reactive than iron. The block is in electrical contact with the iron. With a scratch, the zinc coating still protects the iron but a tin coating does not.
notes: Chemistry only (4.10.3).

name: Composite material (fibres in a matrix)
subject: chemistry
draw: A block cut away to show long fibres or rods embedded in a shaded matrix, with the labels reinforcement and matrix. Examples named beside it: glass fibre, reinforced concrete.
params: reinforcement (fibres | rods | particles), matrix shading, label mode
scienceChecks: The reinforcement sits inside the matrix and does not touch the surface in the cut-away.
notes: Nice-to-have. AQA's text lists composites among materials; I did not see a diagram requirement.

name: The Haber process (flow diagram)
subject: chemistry
draw: Boxes and arrows from left to right: hydrogen (from natural gas) and nitrogen (from the air) in the ratio 3 to 1 enter a compressor, then the reactor (iron catalyst, about 450 degrees C, about 200 atmospheres), then a cooler or condenser where ammonia liquefies and is taken off at the bottom. A return pipe carries unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen back to the compressor. The equation N2 + 3H2 reversible arrow 2NH3 is written under the reactor.
params: show conditions (boolean), show the recycle pipe (boolean), show the sources of the gases (boolean), label mode (names | blank)
scienceChecks: The feed gases are in the ratio 1 nitrogen to 3 hydrogen. The recycle pipe returns the unreacted gases to before the reactor. Ammonia leaves as a liquid after cooling. The equation is balanced.
notes: Chemistry only. AQA shows a labelled reactor and separator in an exam question. Conditions given are the usual textbook values; sources differ a little on the pressure.

name: Making NPK fertilisers from ammonia, acids and potassium salts
subject: chemistry
draw: Boxes and arrows: ammonia reacting with nitric acid to give ammonium nitrate; phosphate rock treated with nitric or sulfuric acid to give soluble phosphates; potassium chloride or sulfate from mining; the three combined into an NPK fertiliser. Each box labelled with the nutrient (N, P or K).
params: label mode, show the nutrients (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each salt contains the nutrient named: N in ammonium nitrate, P in the phosphate, K in the potassium salt. The acids used for phosphate rock are nitric or sulfuric acid.
notes: Chemistry only. AQA mentions the acid treatment of phosphate rock in the text; the pathway drawing is a teaching convention.

name: Bar chart of the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium content of fertilisers
subject: chemistry
draw: A bar chart with fertiliser types along the bottom and percentage by mass up the side, grouped bars for N, P and K. An AQA question asks students to draw the bars from a table and to explain why the percentages do not add to 100.
params: fertilisers, values, which bars are blank
scienceChecks: Each fertiliser's percentages sum to less than 100 because other elements are present.
notes: Chart: outside PracDraw unless James brings charts into scope.

name: Small molecules with covalent bonds inside and weak forces between them
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Four to six small molecules (methane, water, carbon dioxide or iodine) arranged in a loose pattern. The covalent bonds inside each molecule are solid lines. The weak forces between neighbouring molecules are dotted lines with the label 'weak forces between molecules'. A second picture of a giant covalent structure beside it, with only solid lines, for comparison.
params: molecule (methane | water | carbon dioxide | iodine | ammonia), molecules shown (4 to 8), compare with a giant structure (boolean)
scienceChecks: Bonds inside a molecule are solid lines and forces between molecules are dotted. The atom counts of each molecule match its formula. The molecules do not overlap.
notes: Explains why simple molecular substances melt and boil at low temperatures. Uses the ball-and-stick engine.

name: Hazard symbols (the nine GHS pictograms)
subject: chemistry
draw: A square set on its corner (a diamond) with a black outline and a black picture inside: exploding bomb, flame, flame over a circle, gas cylinder, corrosion (liquid on a hand and a metal), skull and crossbones, exclamation mark, health hazard (a body outline with a burst), and environment (a dead tree and a fish). The name in words under each. In colour the border is red; in black-and-white it stays a plain black outline.
params: hazard (explosive | flammable | oxidising | gas under pressure | corrosive | toxic | harmful or irritant | health hazard | hazardous to the environment), show the name (boolean)
scienceChecks: There are nine pictograms. Each has a distinct inner picture and the diamond outline. The name matches the picture.
notes: Already in the Later table of the catalogue (hazardSymbols). Used on risk assessments and in practical lessons. A red border would break the black-line rule (S6); a decision for James. From memory.

name: Time-of-flight mass spectrometer (block diagram)
subject: chemistry
draw: A block diagram from left to right: sample inlet, ionisation (electron gun or electrospray), acceleration between charged plates, a long flight tube kept under vacuum, a detector, then a data system. Two ion paths of different mass are drawn with arrival marks, the lighter one arriving first. Each block has its name and a one-line job.
params: ionisation method (electron impact | electrospray), show the vacuum (boolean), show light and heavy ions (boolean), label mode (names | blank)
scienceChecks: Ionisation comes before acceleration. All ions gain the same kinetic energy in the acceleration. The flight tube is under vacuum. Lighter ions reach the detector first.
notes: AQA names the stages: ionisation, acceleration to give all ions constant kinetic energy, ion drift, detection and data analysis.

name: Mass spectrum of an element or a molecule (bar chart)
subject: chemistry
draw: A bar chart with m/z along the bottom and relative abundance (or percentage) up the side: vertical lines at the isotope masses (for example chlorine at 35 and 37, or Cl2 at 70, 72 and 74). Students read the relative abundance and calculate the relative atomic mass.
params: element or molecule, isotopes and abundances, scale
scienceChecks: The abundances sum to 100 percent (or the stated total). The relative atomic mass equals the weighted mean of the isotope masses. Peaks of a diatomic molecule appear at the sums of isotope masses.
notes: Spectrum: outside PracDraw unless James brings spectra into scope. AQA asks students to interpret simple mass spectra of elements and calculate the relative atomic mass.

name: Electron configuration in sub-shell boxes (s, p and d) with spin arrows
subject: chemistry
draw: A row of boxes for each sub-shell (one box for s, three for p, five for d) labelled 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p. An up arrow or a down arrow in a box is an electron; a full box has one of each. The sub-shell notation (1s2 2s2 2p6 ...) is written beside it. For an ion, the electrons removed or added are shown.
params: element or ion (Z up to 36), charge, notation (boxes | text | both), show only the outer sub-shells (boolean)
scienceChecks: The total of arrows equals Z minus the charge. The order of filling is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p. A box holds at most two electrons with opposite spins. Degenerate boxes fill singly before pairing. Chromium and copper take the half-filled and filled 3d forms. Transition metal ions lose 4s electrons first.
notes: AQA asks for the configurations of atoms and ions up to Z = 36 in terms of shells and sub-shells. The text I read did not say whether box diagrams are required; teachers use them for Hund's rule.

name: Energy levels of sub-shells (1s to 4p) with electrons
subject: chemistry
draw: A vertical energy ladder with a short line for each sub-shell, ordered 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, the gaps shrinking upwards so that 4s sits below 3d. Arrows for electrons on the lines for the chosen element.
params: element or ion, show the order of filling (boolean)
scienceChecks: 4s is lower than 3d. The level count per sub-shell is 1 for s, 3 for p, 5 for d. The electron total equals Z minus the charge.

name: Shapes of s and p orbitals
subject: chemistry
draw: A sphere for an s orbital and a pair of lobes (dumbbell) for each p orbital along the x, y and z axes, on a set of three axes. Outline only, no shading (S1, S7). Optional: an s orbital inside a larger s orbital.
params: orbital (1s | 2s | 2px | 2py | 2pz | all three p), show axes (boolean)
scienceChecks: The three p orbitals are at right angles. An s orbital is spherical. The lobes of a p orbital are equal in size and touch at the nucleus.
notes: I could not confirm whether the AQA 7405 text asks students to draw orbital shapes. Teachers draw them when explaining sigma and pi bonds.

name: Ionisation energy graphs (successive, and across Period 3 or down Group 2)
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes: ionisation energy (or its logarithm) up the side. Successive ionisation energies: points for the 1st to the nth ionisation of one element with large jumps where an inner shell is reached. Trend graphs: first ionisation energy against atomic number across Period 3, with dips at aluminium and sulfur. Students mark a point for a stated ionisation.
params: element, number of ionisations, trend (period 3 | group 2), mark a point (boolean)
scienceChecks: Successive ionisation energies increase, with a large jump after the outer electrons. Across Period 3 the first ionisation energy rises overall with dips at aluminium and sulfur. Down Group 2 it falls.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. An AQA paper asks students to put a cross on the figure for the second ionisation energy of silicon.

name: Dot-and-cross diagrams with dative bonds and expanded octets
subject: chemistry
draw: As the GCSE covalent dot-and-cross, but for ions and molecules with a dative bond: both electrons of the shared pair come from the donor and are drawn with the same mark; in a displayed formula the dative bond is an arrow pointing away from the donor. Examples: ammonium, oxonium, ammonia-boron trifluoride, carbon monoxide, aluminium chloride dimer. Expanded octets: sulfur hexafluoride (12 electrons), phosphorus pentachloride (10) and electron-deficient boron trifluoride (6). Ions are in square brackets with the charge.
params: species (NH4+ | H3O+ | NH3BF3 | CO | Al2Cl6 | SF6 | PCl5 | BF3 | BeCl2), mark style (dot and cross | all dots), show dative arrow (boolean)
scienceChecks: Total valence electrons equal the sum of the atoms minus the charge. A dative bond has both electrons from one atom. The central atom has the electron count that its species shows (8, 10, 12 or 6). The ion charge appears outside the brackets.
notes: Same engine as covalentDotCross with a dative-bond option.

name: Shapes of molecules and ions with bond angles (wedge and dash)
subject: chemistry
draw: The central atom with its bonds drawn as plain lines in the plane of the page, wedges coming towards the viewer and dashes going away. Lone pairs on the central atom as a pair of dots or a lobe. The name of the shape and the bond angle written beside it, with the angle arc drawn. Linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral and square planar. A charge outside square brackets for an ion.
params: bonding pairs (2 to 6), lone pairs (0 to 3), central atom and ligands, charge, show angles (boolean), show lone pairs (boolean)
scienceChecks: Angles: linear 180, trigonal planar 120, tetrahedral 109.5, trigonal pyramidal 107, bent 104.5, trigonal bipyramidal 90 and 120, octahedral 90, square planar 90. A lone pair reduces the bond angle (lone pair - lone pair > lone pair - bonding pair > bonding pair - bonding pair). Electron pairs = bonding pairs + lone pairs. The molecule has the symmetry of its shape.
notes: AQA asks students to deduce shapes of familiar and unfamiliar species with up to six electron pairs and draws POCl3 and ClF4- in exams.

name: Polar bonds and polar molecules (partial charges and dipole arrows)
subject: chemistry
draw: A molecule drawn with its shape (plane, wedge and dash as needed), delta-plus on the less electronegative atom and delta-minus on the more electronegative atom of each polar bond, and a dipole arrow with a cross at the delta-plus end. A net dipole arrow beside the molecule, or a note that the dipoles cancel. Examples: HCl, H2O, CO2 (no net dipole), CH3Cl, CCl4 (none), BF3 (none).
params: molecule (HCl | H2O | CO2 | CH3Cl | CCl4 | BF3 | NH3), show the net dipole (boolean)
scienceChecks: Delta-minus is on the more electronegative atom. A molecule is polar only if the bond dipoles do not cancel by symmetry. The dipole arrow points towards the delta-minus atom.
notes: AQA asks students to use partial charges to show that a bond is polar.

name: Intermolecular forces: London forces, permanent dipoles and hydrogen bonds
subject: chemistry
draw: Pairs or small groups of molecules with a dotted line for the force. London forces: two atoms or molecules with delta-plus and delta-minus labels showing an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole. Permanent dipole - permanent dipole: two HCl molecules aligned delta-plus to delta-minus. Hydrogen bonds: water, ammonia, hydrogen fluoride or ethanol, with the lone pair on the acceptor atom shown, the O-H bond, the delta charges and the hydrogen bond drawn as a dotted line in a straight line through the hydrogen.
params: force (London | permanent dipole | hydrogen bond), molecule (Ar | Cl2 | HCl | H2O | NH3 | HF | ethanol), show lone pairs (boolean), show partial charges (boolean)
scienceChecks: A hydrogen bond needs a hydrogen bonded to N, O or F, and a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of the neighbour. The hydrogen bond line runs through the hydrogen and the lone pair, near 180 degrees at the hydrogen. Partial charges alternate across the dotted line. Covalent bonds are solid and the force is dotted.
notes: An AQA report says students often forget to show the lone pair in a hydrogen bond diagram.

name: Ice (hydrogen-bonded open lattice)
subject: chemistry
draw: Water molecules (an oxygen with two hydrogens) in an oblique view, each linked to four neighbours by hydrogen bonds drawn as dotted lines, forming puckered hexagonal rings with open space in the middle. Covalent O-H bonds solid, hydrogen bonds dotted. Labels: hydrogen bond, covalent bond.
params: molecules shown (a cluster of 6 to 10), view (oblique), show labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each oxygen has two covalent and two hydrogen bonds in a roughly tetrahedral arrangement. The rings have six oxygens. Hydrogen bonds are longer than covalent bonds in the drawing.
notes: AQA lists ice among the structures students draw with specified numbers of particles.

name: Iodine (simple molecular lattice)
subject: chemistry
draw: Iodine molecules drawn as pairs of joined circles on the corners and face centres of a cube in an oblique projection (about 14 molecules), each pair tilted as in the crystal, with a label: weak London forces between molecules. Hidden edges dashed.
params: molecules shown (8 to 14), show the unit cell (boolean), show labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each I2 is two circles joined by a bond. The molecules sit on a face-centred cubic pattern. No bond lines are drawn between molecules.
notes: In AQA's list of structures to draw. The exact crystal pattern drawn in mark schemes was not seen.

name: Magnesium (close-packed metal lattice)
subject: chemistry
draw: Layers of Mg2+ ions (circles marked 2+) packed close together in two layers, the second layer sitting in the hollows of the first, with small delocalised electrons between the ions. A side view and a top view. Labels: positive ion, delocalised electron.
params: layers (2 or 3), ions per layer (6 to 12), show electrons (boolean), view (side | top | oblique)
scienceChecks: Each ion carries a 2+ charge and contributes two delocalised electrons. The second layer sits in the gaps of the first. The ions are equal in size and in contact.
notes: The GCSE metallicBonding row draws the simple version.

name: Hess's law cycle (formation, combustion and bond enthalpy)
subject: chemistry
draw: A triangle or box of species with state symbols: reactants top left, products top right, and the common species (elements, or the combustion products) at the bottom. Arrows between them labelled with the enthalpy changes in kJ per mole. The direct route is one arrow, the indirect route two arrows. The unknown arrow is marked with a question mark. Alternative layout as an energy-level diagram with the arrows up or down.
params: type (formation | combustion | bond enthalpy | custom), layout (cycle | energy levels), values (kJ per mole), unknown arrow (boolean)
scienceChecks: The sum of the enthalpy changes round a closed cycle is zero. For formation data, reaction enthalpy = sum of products minus sum of reactants. For combustion data, reaction enthalpy = sum of reactants minus sum of products. Equations are balanced and arrows run in the direction of the equation. On an energy-level diagram an exothermic step points down.
notes: An AQA report says students muddle the direction of the arrows in a Hess cycle.

name: Born-Haber cycle
subject: chemistry
draw: An energy-level diagram: the elements in their standard states at the base level, then levels for gaseous atoms, gaseous ions and the ionic solid, joined by labelled arrows: atomisation of the metal and of the non-metal (up), first (and second) ionisation energy (up), electron affinity (up or down), lattice formation (down), and the enthalpy of formation from the elements to the solid (down). Species have state symbols and charges. For MgCl2 or Na2O the multiples and the second steps are drawn.
params: compound (NaCl | MgCl2 | Na2O | MgO | CaO), show values (boolean), unknown arrow (boolean), layout (levels | cycle)
scienceChecks: Formation enthalpy = atomisations + ionisation energies + electron affinities + lattice formation. Endothermic steps point up and exothermic steps point down. Stoichiometry is right: two atomisations of chlorine for MgCl2. Charges balance in the ionic solid.
notes: A-level only. With the sodium chloride data in the sources the lattice enthalpy comes out near -776 kJ per mole.

name: Enthalpy cycle for dissolving an ionic solid (lattice and hydration)
subject: chemistry
draw: A triangle: the solid at the top left, the aqueous ions at the top right, the gaseous ions at the bottom. The arrow from solid to gaseous ions is the lattice dissociation enthalpy, from gaseous ions to aqueous ions the hydration enthalpies, and the direct arrow the enthalpy of solution.
params: compound, values, unknown arrow
scienceChecks: Enthalpy of solution = lattice dissociation enthalpy + hydration enthalpies. The cycle closes. Equations are balanced with state symbols.
notes: From memory; the AQA wording on enthalpy of solution was not retrieved.

name: Reaction profile with an intermediate and a rate-determining step
subject: chemistry
draw: As the GCSE reaction profile but with two or three humps and valleys: reactants, a first hump, an intermediate in a valley, a second hump, products. The highest hump is marked as the rate-determining step. Optional dashed lower route with a catalyst. Activation energy arrows for each step.
params: steps (2 or 3), exothermic or endothermic overall, catalyst (boolean), mark the rate-determining step (boolean), transition state marks (boolean)
scienceChecks: The rate-determining step is the highest peak relative to the preceding level. The intermediate sits in a valley between two peaks. Start and end levels are unchanged by a catalyst.
notes: From memory: a reasonable extension of the GCSE profile for rate equations and mechanisms.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves (temperature and catalyst)
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes: number of molecules (or fraction) up the side, energy along the bottom, with no numbers. A curve that starts at the origin, rises to a peak and falls without touching the axis. At a higher temperature the peak is lower and moves right, with the same area under the curve. A vertical line for the activation energy, and a second, lower line for the catalysed reaction, with the extra area shaded.
params: temperatures (1 or 2), activation energy line (boolean), catalysed line (boolean), shade the area (boolean)
scienceChecks: The curve starts at the origin and never touches the axis again. The area under each curve is the same. A hotter curve has a lower peak at a higher energy. The catalysed activation energy line is to the left of the uncatalysed one.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. This is a sketch with no data; a parametric sketch symbol would be an alternative to a chart tool. AQA reports show students mixing up the axis labels.

name: Concentration against time (tangents, order and half-life)
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes with scales: concentration up, time along. A falling curve with tangents at stated times and the gradient triangles; for first-order curves a series of equal half-lives marked; for zero order a straight line.
params: order (0 | 1 | 2), tangent times, half-life marks (boolean)
scienceChecks: A zero-order curve is a straight line. A first-order curve has constant half-lives. A tangent touches the curve at one point and its gradient is the rate.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. AQA asks students to draw tangents to concentration-time curves.

name: Rate against concentration graphs (zero, first and second order)
subject: chemistry
draw: Three small graphs of rate against concentration: a horizontal line for zero order, a straight line through the origin for first order, and a curve rising faster than a straight line for second order, each labelled with its order. Students use them to deduce the order.
params: order (0 | 1 | 2), data points, line of best fit
scienceChecks: Zero order is horizontal. First order is a straight line through the origin. Second order is a curve through the origin that steepens.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope.

name: Gibbs free energy change against temperature
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes: free energy change up (with zero marked), temperature in kelvin along. A straight line whose intercept is the enthalpy change and whose gradient is minus the entropy change; the temperature where the line crosses zero is marked as the point where the reaction becomes feasible.
params: enthalpy change, entropy change, which quantity is read from the graph
scienceChecks: The gradient is minus the entropy change. The intercept at 0 K is the enthalpy change. The reaction is feasible where the free energy change is below zero.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. AQA asks students to determine the entropy change and the enthalpy change from the graph.

name: Temperature-time graph with extrapolation (calorimetry)
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes with scales: temperature up, time along. Points for a reading before the reaction, then after mixing; a line of best fit through the cooling points extended back to the time of mixing to find the temperature change that would have occurred without heat loss.
params: readings, time of mixing, extrapolated line (boolean)
scienceChecks: The extrapolated line is drawn through the cooling points only. The temperature change is read at the time of mixing.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. From memory of the enthalpy practical.

name: pH curves for titrations (strong and weak acids and bases)
subject: chemistry
draw: Axes: pH (0 to 14) up the side, volume of added solution along the bottom. Four S-shaped curves for strong acid with strong base, weak acid with strong base, strong acid with weak base and weak acid with weak base, each with its steep rise at the equivalence point marked and the range of a suitable indicator shown as a band. For the weak acid curve a buffer region and the half-equivalence point are marked.
params: combination (strong-strong | weak acid-strong base | strong acid-weak base | weak-weak), direction (acid into base | base into acid), indicator band (boolean), mark equivalence (boolean)
scienceChecks: A strong acid with a strong base rises through pH 7 at equivalence. A weak acid with a strong base has its equivalence point above 7 and a start at a higher pH than a strong acid. A strong acid with a weak base has its equivalence point below 7. An indicator is suitable when its colour range lies within the steep part.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. AQA asks students to sketch and explain the curves and to select indicators. The pH meter set-up is the existing phCurve template.

name: Standard hydrogen electrode and half-cell diagrams
subject: chemistry
draw: A glass jacket with a platinum electrode (platinised foil) dipping into a solution of 1.00 mol per dm3 hydrogen ions, hydrogen gas at 100 kPa bubbled in through a side tube and escaping from the top, connected through a salt bridge to the second half-cell, with a high-resistance voltmeter between the two electrodes. Labels give 298 K, 100 kPa and 1.00 mol per dm3.
params: second half-cell (Cu2+ and Cu | Zn2+ and Zn | custom), show conditions (boolean), show voltmeter (boolean)
scienceChecks: The standard conditions are all stated: 298 K, 100 kPa, 1.00 mol per dm3. The hydrogen electrode has gas supplied and the platinum electrode is in contact with both gas and solution. The salt bridge connects the two solutions. The potential of the hydrogen half-cell is 0.00 V.
notes: AQA asks for the IUPAC cell notation (Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s)), which is text. The existing electrochemicalCell template is the two-beaker version without the gas electrode.

name: Electrode potential series (vertical scale of standard potentials)
subject: chemistry
draw: A vertical list of half-equations with their standard electrode potentials, the most negative at the top, with arrows for strongest reducing agent (top left) and strongest oxidising agent (bottom right). Students predict the direction of a reaction and the cell potential.
params: half-equations shown, potentials
scienceChecks: The list is in order of potential. The cell potential = more positive minus more negative potential.
notes: Table: outside PracDraw unless James brings tables into scope. From memory.

name: Period 3 trends (atomic radius, first ionisation energy, melting point)
subject: chemistry
draw: A line or bar graph with the elements sodium to argon along the bottom and one property up the side: atomic radius falling, first ionisation energy rising with dips at aluminium and sulfur, melting point rising to a peak at silicon then falling. Students explain each in terms of structure and bonding.
params: property (atomic radius | first ionisation energy | melting point | electronegativity), show structure labels (giant metallic | giant covalent | molecular) (boolean)
scienceChecks: Radius falls across the period. Melting point peaks at silicon (giant covalent). First ionisation energy dips at aluminium and sulfur.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. AQA asks for the trends in atomic radius, first ionisation energy and melting point of Na to Ar.

name: Phosphorus (P4) and sulfur (S8) molecules
subject: chemistry
draw: P4: four phosphorus atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron, six P-P bonds as solid lines with the hidden bond dashed. S8: eight sulfur atoms in a puckered crown-shaped ring drawn in perspective. Drawn with the same oblique projection as the other 3D structures.
params: molecule (P4 | S8 | Cl2 | Ar as a single atom), show bond angles (boolean)
scienceChecks: P4 has four atoms, six bonds, each atom with three bonds. S8 has eight atoms in a ring, each with two bonds. The ring is not flat.
notes: Needed to explain the melting points of the Period 3 non-metals. From memory; not seen in a source.

name: Oxoacids and oxoanions of phosphorus and sulfur (displayed formulae)
subject: chemistry
draw: Displayed formulae with every bond: phosphoric(V) acid, sulfuric(IV) acid and sulfuric(VI) acid, each with P=O or S=O double bonds and O-H bonds, and the anions they form (phosphate, sulfite, sulfate) in square brackets with the charge, the lost hydrogen shown as O-. Optional tetrahedral 3D versions with wedge and dash. Equations beside them for the oxides reacting with water.
params: species (H3PO4 | H2SO3 | H2SO4 | PO4 3- | SO3 2- | SO4 2-), 2D or 3D, show the oxide equation (boolean)
scienceChecks: The anion charge equals the number of O- groups. Phosphate and sulfate have four oxygens on the central atom and sulfite three. Hydrogens sit on oxygen atoms only. Atoms are conserved in the oxide equations.
notes: AQA says students must know the structures of the acids and anions formed when P4O10, SO2 and SO3 react with water.

name: Phosphorus(V) oxide molecule (P4O10 cage)
subject: chemistry
draw: A tetrahedron of four phosphorus atoms with an oxygen bridging each of the six edges and one more oxygen (double bonded) on each phosphorus, in the oblique projection. Phosphorus and oxygen distinguished by size and fill.
params: show the key (boolean), show the tetrahedron edges (boolean)
scienceChecks: Four P and ten O atoms. Each P has three bridging O and one terminal O (four bonds counting the double bond). Each bridging O joins two P.
notes: Nice-to-have. From memory.

name: Shapes of complex ions (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar, linear)
subject: chemistry
draw: The metal ion at the centre, the ligands round it joined by lines, wedges and dashes, the whole inside square brackets with the overall charge outside. Octahedral: [Cu(H2O)6]2+ with two bonds in the plane, two wedges, two dashes. Tetrahedral: [CuCl4]2-. Square planar: [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] and [PtCl4]2-. Linear: [Ag(NH3)2]+. The coordinate (dative) bonds may carry arrows from the ligand lone pair to the metal. Bond angles labelled.
params: shape (octahedral | tetrahedral | square planar | linear), central ion, ligand, charge, show angles (boolean), show dative arrows (boolean)
scienceChecks: The coordination number equals the number of dative bonds (2, 4, 4 or 6). The overall charge equals the metal charge plus the ligand charges. Angles: octahedral 90, tetrahedral 109.5, square planar 90, linear 180. The bond is drawn to the donor atom of the ligand (O in water, N in ammonia).
notes: AQA mark schemes award marks for 6-coordinate and 4-coordinate diagrams. Large ligands such as chloride give tetrahedral complexes with four ligands.

name: Ligands: monodentate, bidentate and EDTA (donor atoms marked)
subject: chemistry
draw: Displayed formulae of ligands with the lone pair on each donor atom drawn as a pair of dots or a lobe: water, ammonia, chloride, hydroxide; 1,2-diaminoethane (two nitrogens) and ethanedioate (two oxygens) as bidentate; EDTA4- with its six donor atoms marked. Optionally the ligand shown bound to a metal ion as a ring (chelate).
params: ligand (water | ammonia | chloride | hydroxide | en | ethanedioate | EDTA), show donor atoms (boolean), show bound to a metal (boolean)
scienceChecks: Denticity equals the number of donor atoms that bind (en 2, ethanedioate 2, EDTA 6). Each donor atom has a lone pair. Ligand charges: ethanedioate 2-, EDTA 4-.

name: Isomers of complex ions (cis-trans and optical)
subject: chemistry
draw: Square planar cis- and trans-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2] (cisplatin and its isomer) drawn side by side. Octahedral cis- and trans-[Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ drawn with wedge and dash. The mirror-image pair of [Ni(en)3]2+ with three bidentate ligands drawn as arcs between the metal and the donor atoms, a dashed mirror line between them. Labels name the isomer.
params: complex (cisplatin | Co(NH3)4Cl2 | Ni(en)3), isomer pair, mirror plane (boolean)
scienceChecks: Cis has the two identical ligands adjacent, trans opposite. The optical pair are mirror images that cannot be superimposed. Each isomer pair has the same formula and the same coordination number.
notes: AQA mark schemes award marks for cis and trans diagrams for square planar and octahedral complexes and describe cisplatin as the cis isomer.

name: d-orbital splitting in an octahedral or tetrahedral complex (colour)
subject: chemistry
draw: A vertical energy diagram: the five d orbitals as short lines at one level on the left (free ion), splitting on the right into two groups with a gap labelled the energy difference. Octahedral: three lower, two higher. Tetrahedral: two lower, three higher. Electrons as arrows. A wavy arrow for an absorbed photon from the lower to the higher group, labelled with the energy relation (energy difference = h times frequency). A note that the colour seen is the colour not absorbed.
params: geometry (octahedral | tetrahedral), d electrons (0 to 10), ligand strength (weak | strong, changes the gap), show the photon (boolean)
scienceChecks: The octahedral split is 3 below and 2 above, the tetrahedral 2 below and 3 above. The energy difference equals h times frequency. A d0 or d10 ion has no d to d transition and is colourless. A stronger-field ligand makes the gap larger.
notes: AQA says colour comes from absorbed light and gives the energy relation; the energy diagram itself was not confirmed in the AQA text I read.

name: Colorimeter (block diagram) and calibration graph
subject: chemistry
draw: A light source, a filter of the complementary colour, a cuvette with the sample, a detector and a meter in a row, with arrows for the light beam. Beside it a calibration graph of absorbance against concentration, a straight line through the origin, with the reading for an unknown marked.
params: filter colour, show the graph (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: The filter colour is complementary to the colour of the solution. The cuvette is between the filter and the detector. The calibration line passes through the origin.
notes: AQA suggests determining the copper(II) ion concentration by colorimetry; the instrument drawing is not an AQA requirement. A graph is outside PracDraw unless James decides otherwise.

name: Heterogeneous catalysis on a metal surface (adsorption, reaction, desorption)
subject: chemistry
draw: Three or four panels from left to right: reactant molecules approaching a row of metal atoms; the molecules adsorbed on the surface with their bonds weakened (dotted); the reaction on the surface; product molecules leaving the surface. Optional fifth panel: a poison blocking active sites. Arrows between the panels.
params: reaction (N2 + 3H2 | CO + NO | custom), show poisoning (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: Atoms are conserved across the panels. The catalyst atoms are unchanged. Adsorption comes before reaction and desorption after.
notes: AQA names the Haber process iron catalyst and catalytic converters as examples.

name: Reaction scheme of aqua ions with hydroxide and ammonia
subject: chemistry
draw: A branching scheme: the hexaaqua ion in the centre, an arrow with sodium hydroxide to the neutral hydroxide precipitate (colour and formula), a further arrow with excess hydroxide or ammonia to a dissolved complex (for aluminium, copper, iron(III)). Each species has its formula, charge and colour. For Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+ and Al3+.
params: metal ion (Cu2+ | Fe2+ | Fe3+ | Al3+), reagents (NaOH | NH3), show colours (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: Hydroxide precipitates are neutral. Charges and atoms balance in every step. Only aluminium (and copper with ammonia) dissolve in excess as the scheme shows. Colours: Cu2+ blue, Fe2+ green, Fe3+ brown precipitate, Al3+ white.
notes: The AQA teaching guide says some cobalt(II) colours are no longer required; vanadium colours still are.

name: Why hexaaqua ions are acidic (polarised water ligand)
subject: chemistry
draw: An octahedral hexaaqua ion with one water ligand enlarged: the metal ion pulling electron density from the oxygen, the O-H bond polarised, and an arrow showing a hydrogen ion leaving to a free water molecule. Two panels for a 2+ and a 3+ ion; the 3+ ion pulls harder and its arrows are bolder.
params: ion charge (2+ | 3+), show the equilibrium equation (boolean)
scienceChecks: The 3+ ion has a larger charge-to-size ratio and gives the more acidic solution. The hydrolysis equation balances in atoms and charge.
notes: AQA asks students to explain the acidity in terms of the charge-to-size ratio; the picture form is a teaching convention from memory.

name: Skeletal formula of an organic molecule
subject: chemistry
draw: Zig-zag lines with a carbon at every corner and at the end of every line (the carbon is not labelled) and the hydrogens on carbon left out. Other atoms and groups written in full at the end of a bond (OH, NH2, Cl, Br, CHO, COOH, CO2CH3), written so that the correct atom is joined. Double bonds as two parallel lines, rings as regular polygons, benzene as a hexagon with a circle or three double bonds. Wedge and dash bonds at a chiral centre. Chain bonds at 120 degrees. Used for chains and rings of up to six carbons.
params: molecule from a library (alkanes, alkenes, halogenoalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amines, amides, nitriles and benzene derivatives, with a main chain or ring of up to six carbons), stereo bonds (boolean), show implied hydrogens (boolean), name beside it (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every carbon has four bonds counting implied hydrogens. Hetero atoms are labelled and carbon is not. Chain bonds meet at 120 degrees. The molecular formula derived from the drawing equals the stated formula. A ring has the stated number of corners.
notes: Skeletal formulae are out of scope in section 4 of the specification, so this is a decision for James. AQA asks students to draw structural, displayed and skeletal formulae from names and to name from drawings.

name: Structural isomers (chain, position and functional group)
subject: chemistry
draw: A row of skeletal or displayed formulae that share one molecular formula, each with its name under it: for example butane and methylpropane (chain), pentan-1-ol and pentan-2-ol (position), ethanol and methoxymethane (functional group). The molecular formula in a heading.
params: molecular formula (C4H10 | C5H12 | C4H9Br | C3H6O | C2H6O), isomer set to show, style (skeletal | displayed), blank some for a worksheet
scienceChecks: Every drawing has the same molecular formula. No two drawings are the same molecule. Known counts: C4H10 has 2, C5H12 has 3 and C4H9Br has 4 structural isomers.
notes: Uses the skeletal formula engine.

name: E/Z isomers (cis and trans)
subject: chemistry
draw: The two isomers of an alkene side by side as skeletal formulae with the double bond in the plane. The priority atoms on each carbon marked. Z has the higher-priority groups on the same side, E on opposite sides. The labels E and Z (and cis, trans where they apply) beside each. A note that rotation about the double bond is restricted.
params: alkene (but-2-ene | pent-2-ene | 1,2-dichloroethene | custom), show priority marks (boolean), label (E and Z | cis and trans | both)
scienceChecks: Each carbon of the double bond has two different groups. The higher-priority groups (by atomic number, then the next atom out) are on the same side in Z and on opposite sides in E. The two drawings are different molecules with the same formula.
notes: An AQA paper asks students to draw the E and Z forms of a structural isomer of C5H10O that shows both E/Z and optical isomerism.

name: Optical isomers (enantiomers with wedge and dash bonds)
subject: chemistry
draw: A carbon with four different groups: two bonds in the plane of the page, one wedge and one dash, the centre marked with a star. The mirror-image molecule on the right, with a dashed vertical mirror line between the two, and a note that the two cannot be superimposed. Examples: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, 2-chlorobutane, a simple amino acid.
params: molecule (2-hydroxypropanoic acid | 2-chlorobutane | alanine | CHFClBr), mirror line (boolean), mark the chiral centre (boolean)
scienceChecks: The marked carbon has four different groups. The right-hand drawing is the mirror image of the left. Swapping two groups on one drawing gives the other. A molecule with two identical groups on the carbon is reported as not chiral.
notes: AQA says students draw 3D representations of chiral centres and explain racemic mixtures.

name: Curly arrow (movement of an electron pair, or of one electron)
subject: chemistry
draw: A curved line (one smooth curve) with a full arrowhead for a pair of electrons and a half arrowhead (fish-hook) for one electron. It starts on a bond, a lone pair or a negative charge and ends on an atom or on the middle of a bond where a new bond forms. The curve bends away from the rest of the structure, with an adjustable bend.
params: start (bond | lone pair | negative charge | radical dot), end (atom | bond | between atoms), head (full | half), bend (-1 to 1)
scienceChecks: The tail starts on a source of electrons and never on a positive charge. The head ends on an electron-poor atom or at the place where a new bond forms. A full head moves two electrons and a half head one. The curve does not cross the structure's own atoms.
notes: A new kind of connector for the editor (section 10 of the specification has four kinds, none of them curved). AQA says radical mechanisms need a dot for the unpaired electron and do not need curly arrows.

name: Mechanism: free radical substitution (initiation, propagation, termination)
subject: chemistry
draw: Three labelled groups of equations drawn with the structures: initiation (Cl-Cl splits into two chlorine radicals in ultraviolet light), propagation (a chlorine radical takes a hydrogen from methane to give HCl and a methyl radical; the methyl radical takes a chlorine from Cl2 to give chloromethane and a chlorine radical), termination (two radicals combine). Each radical has a dot beside its atom. Optional fish-hook arrows.
params: alkane (methane | ethane), halogen (chlorine | bromine), show the stage names (boolean), show fish-hook arrows (boolean), further substitution (boolean)
scienceChecks: A radical carries a dot on the atom with the unpaired electron. Atoms are conserved in every step. Each propagation step uses one radical and makes one radical. Termination steps use two radicals and make none. Initiation makes two radicals from a molecule.

name: Mechanism: electrophilic addition to an alkene (via a carbocation)
subject: chemistry
draw: Step 1: the C=C of the alkene attacks the delta-plus hydrogen of H-Br with a curly arrow from the double bond, a second arrow from the H-Br bond to the bromine, giving a carbocation (positive charge on the carbon) and a bromide ion. Step 2: a curly arrow from a lone pair on the bromide ion to the positive carbon, giving the bromoalkane. For an unsymmetrical alkene both routes are drawn and the more stable (more substituted) carbocation is marked as the major one. Charges and lone pairs shown.
params: alkene (ethene | propene | but-2-ene), reagent (HBr | Br2 with an induced dipole), show both routes (boolean), mark major and minor product (boolean)
scienceChecks: The first arrow starts at the pi bond. The second arrow starts at the H-Br bond and ends on bromine. The carbocation carries a plus and the bromide a minus with lone pairs. The tertiary carbocation is more stable than the secondary, then the primary. Atoms and charge are conserved.
notes: Listed in the AQA text as one of the mechanisms; the detail drawn is the usual textbook form.

name: Mechanism: nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane (SN2 and SN1)
subject: chemistry
draw: SN2 (primary): a curly arrow from the lone pair on the nucleophile (OH-, CN- or NH3) to the delta-plus carbon, a second arrow from the C-X bond to the halogen, with the transition state in square brackets (partial bonds dotted, a double dagger mark and the charge). SN1 (tertiary): the halide leaves first as a curly arrow from the C-X bond to X, giving a carbocation, then the nucleophile attacks. The product and the halide ion shown.
params: halogenoalkane (primary | tertiary), nucleophile (OH- | CN- | NH3 | H2O), mechanism (SN2 | SN1), show the transition state (boolean)
scienceChecks: The first arrow starts at the nucleophile's lone pair and ends on the carbon. The second arrow starts at the C-X bond and ends on X. In SN2 the carbon has five partial bonds in the transition state. In SN1 a carbocation intermediate appears. Primary halogenoalkanes use SN2 and tertiary use SN1. Charge and atoms are conserved.

name: Mechanism: elimination of hydrogen halide from a halogenoalkane
subject: chemistry
draw: Three curly arrows on a halogenoalkane: from the lone pair of the hydroxide ion (acting as a base, in ethanolic solution) to a hydrogen on the carbon next to the C-X carbon; from that C-H bond to form the C=C; from the C-X bond to the halogen, giving the alkene, water and the halide ion.
params: halogenoalkane (2-bromopropane | bromoethane | 2-bromobutane), show all possible alkenes (boolean)
scienceChecks: The hydrogen removed is on the carbon next to the carbon bearing the halogen. The C=C forms between those two carbons. Atoms and charge are conserved. For 2-bromobutane more than one alkene is possible.

name: Mechanism: nucleophilic addition to an aldehyde or ketone (cyanide, hydride)
subject: chemistry
draw: The carbonyl group drawn with its polarity (delta-plus carbon, delta-minus oxygen). A curly arrow from the lone pair on the cyanide ion (or the hydride ion from the reducing agent) to the carbon; a second arrow from the C=O pi bond to the oxygen, giving an intermediate with O-; then a curly arrow from the oxygen lone pair to H+ (from water or acid) giving the hydroxynitrile (or the alcohol). Both enantiomers of the product are drawn for an unsymmetrical carbonyl.
params: carbonyl (ethanal | propanone | propanal), nucleophile (CN- | H- from NaBH4), show both enantiomers (boolean)
scienceChecks: The nucleophile's arrow ends on the carbonyl carbon. The pi bond arrow ends on oxygen. The intermediate carries a negative charge on oxygen. The final step adds H+ to oxygen. The carbonyl carbon is planar, so attack from either face gives a racemic mixture when the carbon becomes chiral.
notes: AQA says aldehydes and unsymmetrical ketones form mixtures of enantiomers with KCN then acid and asks for an explanation.

name: Mechanism: nucleophilic addition-elimination (acyl chlorides)
subject: chemistry
draw: Step 1: a curly arrow from the nucleophile lone pair (water, an alcohol, ammonia or an amine) to the carbonyl carbon of the acyl chloride, a second arrow from the C=O pi bond to oxygen, giving a tetrahedral intermediate with O- and a positive nucleophile atom. Step 2: the C=O re-forms with an arrow from the oxygen lone pair, the chloride leaves with an arrow from the C-Cl bond, and a hydrogen ion is lost to give hydrogen chloride and the product (acid, ester, amide or N-substituted amide).
params: acyl chloride (ethanoyl chloride | propanoyl chloride), nucleophile (water | ethanol | ammonia | methylamine), show the intermediate (boolean)
scienceChecks: The intermediate has a negative oxygen and a positive nucleophile atom with four groups on the carbon. The chloride is the leaving group. Atoms and charge are conserved. The by-product is HCl.
notes: In the AQA list of mechanisms for acyl chlorides and acid anhydrides; the detail is the usual textbook form.

name: Mechanism: electrophilic substitution of benzene (nitration, acylation)
subject: chemistry
draw: First the electrophile is made: NO2+ from concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid (equation), or the acylium ion from an acyl chloride and aluminium chloride. Then the benzene ring with a curly arrow from the delocalised ring to the electrophile; the intermediate drawn as a ring with a horseshoe of dashes over five carbons, a plus charge inside it, and the H and the new group on the sp3 carbon; a curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring, the hydrogen ion leaving, and the catalyst (sulfuric acid or aluminium chloride) regenerated.
params: reaction (nitration | Friedel-Crafts acylation), show the electrophile step (boolean), show the catalyst regeneration (boolean)
scienceChecks: The electrophile (NO2+ or the acylium ion) is made first. In the intermediate the ring is not aromatic and has a plus charge delocalised over five carbons. The hydrogen lost is the one on the carbon that took the electrophile. The catalyst is regenerated. Atoms and charge are conserved.
notes: AQA names nitration and acylation as the electrophilic substitution mechanisms.

name: Benzene: Kekule structure, delocalised ring and p-orbital overlap
subject: chemistry
draw: Three pictures: the Kekule hexagon with alternating double and single bonds; the delocalised ring (hexagon with a circle inside); and a side view of the planar carbon skeleton with six p orbitals as lobes above and below the ring overlapping into a ring of electron density. Labels: all bonds equal, 120 degrees, planar.
params: view (Kekule | delocalised | orbital overlap | all three), show hydrogens (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: Six carbons and six hydrogens. Bond angles 120 degrees. The delocalised picture has six equal bonds. The p orbital picture has six lobes above and below the plane.

name: Enthalpy of hydrogenation levels: evidence for delocalisation in benzene
subject: chemistry
draw: An energy-level diagram: cyclohexane at the bottom, benzene a little above the line predicted for three isolated double bonds, and cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene (hypothetical) higher still; arrows for the enthalpy changes of hydrogenation of cyclohexene, the predicted value for three double bonds and the measured value for benzene, and a labelled gap for the extra stability.
params: show the values (boolean), show the gap labelled as stabilisation (boolean)
scienceChecks: The measured hydrogenation enthalpy of benzene is less exothermic in size than three times that of cyclohexene. The gap equals the difference.
notes: From memory; the AQA text on the evidence for delocalisation was not retrieved.

name: Condensation polymers: polyester and polyamide repeat units (skeletal)
subject: chemistry
draw: The two monomers as skeletal formulae, a reaction arrow, and the polymer chain with the repeat unit in square brackets, the ester or amide links circled, and water (or hydrogen chloride) shown as the small molecule lost. Examples: a polyester from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid (PET), nylon-6,6 from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid, Kevlar.
params: polymer (PET | nylon-6,6 | nylon-6 | Kevlar), show the small molecule lost (boolean), circle the links (boolean), draw two repeat units (boolean)
scienceChecks: One small molecule is lost for every link formed. The repeat unit contains one of each monomer unit. Ester links are -COO- and amide links -CONH-. Atoms are conserved.
notes: AQA exam questions ask students to draw the repeat unit of a polyester and a polyamide and to identify monomers from a chain.

name: Triglyceride, soap and biodiesel
subject: chemistry
draw: A triglyceride as a glycerol backbone with three ester links to three long fatty acid chains (saturated or unsaturated, drawn as zig-zags). Arrows to the products of hydrolysis with sodium hydroxide (glycerol and three soap molecules, each a carboxylate with a long chain) or of reaction with methanol (biodiesel, methyl esters, plus glycerol).
params: reaction (hydrolysis to soap | biodiesel), chain length and unsaturation, show the ester links (boolean)
scienceChecks: Three ester links join one glycerol to three fatty acid chains. Hydrolysis gives glycerol and three carboxylates. Atoms and charge are conserved.

name: Amino acid forms (zwitterion, cation, anion) and the peptide link
subject: chemistry
draw: A simple amino acid in three forms joined by arrows labelled with the pH: the cation at low pH (NH3+ and COOH), the zwitterion (NH3+ and COO-) at the isoelectric point, and the anion at high pH (NH2 and COO-). Below it, two amino acids condensing to a dipeptide with the peptide (amide) link circled and water lost.
params: amino acid (glycine | alanine | custom R), show the pH labels (boolean), show the dipeptide (boolean)
scienceChecks: The charges sum to +1 for the cation, 0 for the zwitterion and -1 for the anion. A peptide link is -CONH- and one water is lost for each link formed.
notes: The text of 3.3.13 was not retrieved from AQA; the detail drawn is the usual textbook form.

name: Protein structure (primary, secondary and tertiary)
subject: chemistry
draw: A chain of amino acid residues (primary), a helix and a pleated sheet with the hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups as dotted lines (secondary), and a folded chain held by hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions and sulfur-sulfur bridges (tertiary). Labels name each interaction.
params: level (primary | secondary helix | secondary sheet | tertiary), label mode
scienceChecks: Hydrogen bonds link a C=O oxygen to an N-H hydrogen. A disulfide bridge joins two cysteine sulfurs. The chain has one amino end and one carboxyl end.
notes: From memory; the AQA text on protein structure was not retrieved.

name: DNA base pairs and the sugar-phosphate backbone (displayed)
subject: chemistry
draw: The four bases as skeletal formulae. Adenine and thymine side by side with two hydrogen bonds (dotted); guanine and cytosine with three. Each base attached to a deoxyribose sugar, and the sugars joined by phosphate groups to give the backbone, with the 5 and 3 ends marked.
params: pair (A with T | G with C), show the backbone (boolean), show the hydrogen bonds (boolean)
scienceChecks: A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds and G with C through three. Each hydrogen bond runs from an N-H or O-H hydrogen to a lone pair on N or O. The strands run in opposite directions.

name: Cisplatin binding to DNA
subject: chemistry
draw: Cisplatin (square planar platinum with two ammonia and two chloride ligands) with the two chloride ligands replaced by two nitrogen atoms of neighbouring guanine bases on one strand of DNA, which bends the double helix. A before and after pair.
params: show the ligand substitution (boolean), label mode
scienceChecks: The two cis ligands are the ones replaced. The platinum stays square planar with two NH3 and two N donors from the bases.

name: Enzyme active site and competitive inhibition
subject: chemistry
draw: An enzyme as a blob with a notch (the active site), a substrate with a matching shape fitting into it, the products leaving. A second panel with an inhibitor of similar shape in the site and the substrate blocked. Enantiomers: one fits, its mirror image does not.
params: panel (substrate | inhibitor | enantiomer), label mode
scienceChecks: The substrate and active site shapes match. The inhibitor shape matches the site. The wrong enantiomer does not fit.
notes: From memory; an AQA paper asks how an enzyme selects one enantiomer.

name: Multi-step organic synthesis route (reagents and conditions)
subject: chemistry
draw: Boxes for compounds (names and skeletal formulae) joined by arrows, each arrow labelled above with the reagent and below with the conditions (for example reflux, ethanolic KOH, acidified dichromate). Typical starting points: alkene, halogenoalkane, alcohol, aldehyde, carboxylic acid, ester, amine, nitrile.
params: route (from a library of conversions), blank reagents for a worksheet, show conditions (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each arrow is a real conversion of the type named. The carbon count changes only through nitrile formation or similar. The reagent given matches the functional group change.
notes: AQA 3.3.14 asks students to design routes; I could not retrieve the text, so this is from memory.

name: Proton NMR spectrum (shift, splitting, integration)
subject: chemistry
draw: A spectrum drawn right to left with the chemical shift in ppm, the reference peak (TMS) at zero, and peaks as vertical lines or small groups of lines: singlets, doublets, triplets and quartets from the n plus 1 rule, with the integration ratio under each group. Students use it with the data booklet to suggest a structure.
params: molecule, shifts and splitting, show integration (boolean), blank the structure
scienceChecks: A signal with n equivalent neighbouring protons has n plus 1 lines. Integration ratios equal the ratio of equivalent protons. TMS is at zero. The number of signals equals the number of proton environments.
notes: Spectrum: outside PracDraw unless James brings spectra into scope. AQA asks students to use the n plus 1 rule and integration, and to know why TMS is used.

name: Carbon-13 NMR spectrum
subject: chemistry
draw: A spectrum with the chemical shift in ppm, TMS at zero, and one vertical line for each carbon environment. Groups of peaks such as C=O at 160 to 220 ppm and C-O at 50 to 90 ppm are labelled by region. Peak height does not give the number of carbons.
params: molecule, shifts, blank the structure
scienceChecks: The number of peaks equals the number of different carbon environments. Peak heights are not proportional to the carbon count.
notes: Spectrum: outside PracDraw unless James brings spectra into scope.

name: Infrared spectrum (transmittance against wavenumber)
subject: chemistry
draw: A spectrum with percentage transmittance up, wavenumber (cm-1) along from high to low, and downward troughs: a broad trough near 3300 for an alcohol O-H, a very broad trough from 2500 to 3300 for a carboxylic acid O-H, a sharp trough near 1700 for C=O, and a busy fingerprint region below about 1500. Students identify the functional groups.
params: compound, which absorptions are labelled, blank labels
scienceChecks: Wavenumbers decrease left to right. O-H and C=O absorptions fall in their ranges (alcohol O-H 3200 to 3600, acid O-H 2500 to 3300, C=O 1630 to 1820).
notes: Spectrum: outside PracDraw unless James brings spectra into scope. AQA names infrared in 3.3.6; the detail is from revision notes.

name: Mass spectrum of an organic compound (molecular ion and fragments)
subject: chemistry
draw: A bar chart with m/z along the bottom and relative abundance up the side: a molecular ion peak at the relative molecular mass, a small M plus 1 peak, and fragment peaks at characteristic values (15 for CH3+, 29 for C2H5+, 43 for C3H7+ or CH3CO+). Students identify the molecular ion and suggest fragments.
params: compound, which fragments are labelled, blank labels
